speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Marler (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON REQUEST FOR AMENDMENT OF STATUTE TO PROHIBIT DUMPING OF FUEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some days ago the hon. member for Kootenay East, following the accident which occurred to the Venezuelan airliner, asked me if I would consider revising the Aeronautics Act to provide that no dumping of gasoline shall be allowed while aircraft are in flight. I should like to say that I have had the opportunity of conferring with the officials of my department who advise me as follows: It is standard aeronautical practice for aircraft takeoff weights to be in excess of permissible landing weights for the same aircraft, and aircraft operations are based on this practice. This means that if an aircraft with a heavy fuel load is compelled to land sooner than expected and, therefore, has not used up the required amount of fuel it may have to rid itself of this fuel while still in the air before making an emergency landing so as to reduce its weight to the permissible landing weight. In these circumstances, two courses are open. One is for the aircraft to continue flying until it has actually used up the fuel and the other is to dump the fuel while still in the air through emergency valves especially built for this purpose. Fuel dumping in the air is an accepted and necessary safety practice in the event of an emergency landing, particularly where the aircraft has not been able for one reason or another to continue flying so as to use up the fuel.
I should like to make it quite clear, Mr. Speaker, that these remarks do not constitute in any way a judgment as to the cause of the accident to the Venezuelan airliner, as to which we have no information in the department.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Marler (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-STATEMENT RESPECTING CONSIDERATION OF LANGLEY AS SECONDARY AIRPORT
speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for New Westminster referred to the Langley airport. I have been informed that the Langley airport is a useful supplement to the Vancouver international airport and we expect that it would be used for this purpose to an increasing degree in the future, particularly for light aircraft. With this in mind, the federal government has already assisted in the development of the Langley airport and hopes that it may be possible to provide some measure of further assistance in the future. The

Langley airfield, however, will not in itself provide adequate relief for the growing problem of air traffic in the Vancouver area and it is quite clear that an additional airport will have to be developed before long.
I have already announced that if the site at White Rock proves suitable for construction purposes it is our intention to proceed with the development of an airport in that area. Since this announcement was made, I have received some representations against the use of the site at White Rock as an airport and these representations are at present under consideration.

If the hon. member has specific reference to the lower reaches of the Fraser river, solution of this problem may be found to be within the jurisdiction of the New Westminster harbour commissioners since the New Westminster harbour limits include these lower reaches. speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF SALE TO CHINA
speechtext: We have no diplomatic relations with communist China and therefore no official representations have been made or are being made. Inquiries have been made by responsible members of the wheat board about the situation in China, and the information they have received is that China is not at present in the market for either wheat or barley. maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF SALE TO CHINA
speechtext: Does the minister imply, in his reply to the effect that we have no representative in China, that it does interfere with our trading relations with that country?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF SALE TO CHINA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would say very definitely that it interferes with our ability to get official information from that country; however, it does not interfere with any desire that the authorities in China may have of making purchases of foodstuffs in Canada. That can be arranged, but without official representation in China any Canadian who enters that country is on his own. Whether he can approach the proper officials or not depends on his own ingenuity, not on the usual official introductions that he would expect in any other country.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Saint John-Albert last night inquired about hydrographic surveys in southern New Brunswick. We understand from a subsequent conversation with the hon. member that he really means aeromag-netic surveys. A meeting was held in November in Fredericton in which departmental officials participated and arrangements were made to make a survey of southwestern New Brunswick including the counties of Charlotte and part of Queens and Kings. The area was flown in May of this year and the maps that are the result of this survey are now being compiled and will be released as soon as they are completed.
This area is part of the mineral belt of New Brunswick and the aeromagnetic maps will supplement the geological information already available.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, when the announcement was made with respect to this survey it was meant to include Saint John, Kings and Albert counties and it was definitely set up as a southern New Brunswick survey. I have a press clipping here of a conversation that was held with the Minister of Labour and some officials. Perhaps it is not as definite as we might have hoped but it certainly indicated that these counties would be included in the survey and the allocation for this survey would be in the estimates of the department this year. If I could just ask the minister if it is meant to include the counties of Saint John and Albert and when this may begin, it would satisfy me.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I know that this arrangement was made in conjunction with our officials and the officials of the department concerned in New Brunswick. Consultation was held and it was decided what areas should be flown and that has been carried out. My officials here think my hon. friend is correct and that these areas were included although it is not in this statement.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: May I take it then, Mr. Chairman, that this survey which has begun or will begin in the near future is to include in it the county of Saint John and part of Albert?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: The county of Saint John and part of Albert were surveyed-at least that part of it has already been done with respect to these particular counties?

I certainly know very little about hydrographic surveys, but I have talked with those who have experience with these things. I understand that in preparing these charts the charts which were originally prepared by the British admiralty many years ago are used. The British authorities made these original surveys and turned the charts over to this government and now the minister's department is responsible for them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: Yes.

I understand that in many cases the department is still using these old original charts which were prepared perhaps 50, 75 or 100 years ago when they did not have the equipment and scientific data which are available today. I believe the

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys minister does have records to indicate that there are obstructions, rocks and other things which were not indicated on these original charts, and I understand that in fact some departmental ships have encountered such obstructions.
I wonder whether the minister could give the committee some outline of just where this matter stands, how much of this work has been done within recent years and in how many cases are we still dependent upon the old charts which were perhaps made by captains of British frigates cruising around our waters 100 or 150 years ago. It does seem to me that this is a phase of the departmental work which is rather important and if we do have the responsibility for doing all this work now the committee should know how much of it has been brought up to date and how much of it still remains to be done in the years to come before we have a complete and modern set of charts for all of our coastal waters. speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, they are still using a few of the old British admiralty charts but they are being replaced as quickly as possible. I suppose my hon. friend is interested in work being done on the Atlantic coast. The C.G.S. Kapuskasing has a detached party stationed at North Rustico, Prince Edward Island, which has carried out inshore charting off the north shore of the island. The motor launch, Henry Hudson, operating in the Canso area and the motor launch, Anderson, operating in the Liverpool-Cape Raceway area continue to chart the inshore waters off the southern coast of Nova Scotia. As a result a number of hitherto uncharted shoals have been added to the charts of these waters. It is true that these old charts are not entirely accurate. When re-surveys are made reefs are found that are probably just slightly below the safety level, and as fast as possible they are charting these areas, especially where there is heavy shipping.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS

As far as information respecting the northern part of Canada is concerned, what is the procedure? I should preface my remarks by saying that it is essential that other countries, especially the United States, have aerial navigation maps of large areas of this country, if not all of it, and I was wondering what the policy is. Does the government furnish other friendly countries with the required information and do they print their own aerial navigation maps or do we actually sell the maps we have produced to other countries?
This question has arisen in my mind chiefly from looking over an excellent booklet published by the department regarding a profile study of the new Quebec crater. I notice there, if I read it correctly, that the first aerial photograph on which this crater was noted was one taken by the United States air force in 1942 and the first maps on which it appeared were ones produced by the United States air force. Apparently the department also published a map in 1942 with the information on it. Then the following three maps, one produced in 1944 and two in 1945, were also produced by the United States air force.
Appendix B to the booklet would indicate that the first aerial photograph of the crater was taken by trimetrogon survey in 1943 by the United States air force. The first photographs taken by Canada on which the crater appeared were taken by the R.C.A.F. in 1946, three years later. I wonder what the position is. I should like to think that as a nation we have greater and prior knowledge of the northern part of our own country. I think the

question of national pride demands that, if nothing else. Would the minister say a word on that?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: During the period of the war Canada was completely covered by trimetro-gon photography. There was a very urgent need and the United States did co-operate in that particular area of the country, but this department made the maps from that photography. As I said before, trimetrogon photographs were taken and the maps were prepared on the scale of 8 miles to the inch. The R.C.A.F. took up the work as soon as they had the equipment available, and in the last two years we have been doing our photography work by contract. However, I do not think there is any special significance in the fact that the United States took the original photographs of that area, other than the needs of defence.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: I take it that at the present time the United States government publishes its own maps for aerial navigation and we do not supply them with maps produced in Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS

They had a world atlas and they had a map of Canada that was very beautiful and carefully done. We have no control over the mapping that other countries do but we do provide the aeronautical charts for Canada.

I happen to have here a map of Canada. The scale is 100 miles to the inch. It is indicated that it was printed in 1951. I notice that it shows two fairly extensive railways one from Seven Islands up into Labrador and another in Manitoba. They are shown on the map. This is a 1951 map. I am sure that these railways did not exist in 1951. I presume the explanation is that the date of the map should have been changed to some later date and that that was not done when the map was being brought up to date. To me that would indicate sort of sloppy editing, but perhaps there is some other explanation. Then although the key does not show what it is meant to indicate, the map indicates what I take to be a railway under construction or a proposed railway out on the west coast in northern British Columbia just south of the Alaska border. I point that out because I obtained what looks like the same map in French. The French copy of this map is rather interesting to me. It is basically the same map, but I notice that it is dated 1956 and that it shows these two railways as being completed, namely the first two I mentioned, the one in Labrador and the other in Manitoba. However, it does not show this one under construction or whatever is supposed to be represented by this broken red line in B.C. So on looking at the map it would appear that things were in a greater state of advancement in 1951 than in 1956, if you were to take these maps at face value. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Could the minister give us an outline of the more recent developments in connection with the research being carried on by McGill University in an effort to develop a practical coal-fired gas turbine. This is a matter of extreme importance because it is possible that the future of a good deal of
6, 1956	5729
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys our coal industry depends upon the development of a successful turbine of this kind which would provide a market for much of the coal which has been lost through the use of fuel oil in locomotives. This project has been going on for seven or eight years and I do not think we have had any information for the past two or three years as to how close to success it is. I believe a coal-fired turbine was produced as far back as four or five years but there were a number of bugs which had to be ironed out and also the question of producing it in a size which could be used in a locomotive.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
The matter is still in the experimental stage, but Professor Mordell is quite optimistic. He has obtained some fundamental and valuable information from the experiments which have been carried on so far. They have had many difficulties. As I stated in my introductory remarks, they had to make revisions in the heat exchanger and the combustion chamber and so on, but recently they had some success in the continuous operation of the turbine. I received a letter the other day from Professor Mordell saying that they had had a long uninterrupted run. It is necessary to have a large number of hours of continuous operation in order to evaluate fuel savings and economy of operation.
It is proposed to have a symposium this fall of all interested parties in order to make a study of the results obtained to date. I would not like to hazard an opinion as to what the report will be although, as I say, Professor Mordell is quite optimistic. Not being a scientist I have to take his word for it. Certainly they are making an all-out effort to attain success. It took some 50 years to develop the diesel engine to its present stage of perfection, and considering the length of time that this experiment has been under way I think they are making good progress.
It remains to be seen whether it will be of value to the coal industry. Professor Mordell estimates that the fuel saving on a locomotive will be between $20,000 and $50,000 a year, but that remains to be proved. Theoretically that is the possible saving. They are considering the possible application to locomotives as well as to stationary engines for power development purposes. The latest letter I received from Professor Mordell indicates that they will be soon far enough along and have enough information to proceed with the development of a stationary power unit. It is hoped that the symposium will bring out sufficient facts to interest private enterprise in continuing with the development of an engine.

speechtext: Professor Mordell and his associates are very well informed about what is taking place in the United States, Great Britain and other parts of the world. I understand that their experiment has an entirely different approach from that being used in other countries. I understand that in other countries they are driving the hot gases from the combustion of the coal directly through the turbine whereas here they are using heat exchangers which will prevent the fly ash from going directly into the turbine and wearing out or corroding the blades of the turbine. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the minister will remember, I have spoken on this item in other years, and I do think that if there is one place where the department is open to more criticism than others it is in connection with this particular item. As the hon. member for Calgary North said a few moments ago, we have had this item in the estimates now for many years, six or seven years, I think, since we started voting money towards the development of this engine.
I remember that last year the member for Cape Breton South practically stated that in


his opinion it was a fruitless effort and that the development had been so disappointing that nothing more should be expected of it. However, as the minister says, Professor Mordell is very optimistic. Nevertheless, I do not think it is any answer at all for the minister to say that after all it took 10, 15 or 20 years to develop the diesel engine. There was not the great pressure to come ahead with that production because it was at least in competition with existing motive power.
If 50 per cent of the hopes of the people who are close to this project could be realized, it would make the most profound difference to the coal industry of anything that could be accomplished in this country. Whether Professor Mordell is right or not I do not know. As the minister says, he is not a scientist and certainly I am not, but my quarrel is that we have not gone far enough in dealing with this matter one way or the other. Surely we should have had the answers before this. I am not criticizing Professor Mordell at all. I think he has done a wonderful job.
But this matter has been approached from the viewpoint of an experimental project in a university laboratory. That is virtually the approach to it. It is an interesting problem. Let us give them some money and see what they can do with it. I do think, in fairness to the minister, that probably there has not been any great emphasis by Professor Mordell on getting more money. As I said, it has been a matter of a scientific, intellectual experiment which has great possibilities, but let us not disturb the serenity of the laboratory. In the meantime the coal industry is threatened with extinction.
We know that tremendous developments took place during the war in the production of airplanes within a period of months because the resources of the nation were turned loose, bottlenecks were overcome, bugs, to use somebody's expression, were taken out, and you had the project completed. This engine, according to the minister's summary, ran for 300 hours last year. There is some achievement in getting an engine that ran for 300 hours. However, apparently there is trouble with the ash blast, there is some corrosion and there are other problems such as that to be solved.
But Professor Mordell says that this engine is going to be so far ahead of the diesel when he gets it completed that diesels are going to be almost outmoded. I suggested last year that it was most unfortunate that the railways had proceeded so quickly with dieseli-zation when this engine was still in the experimental stage and might even be at the practical stage. I have a statement here

from the press of last summer in which Professor Mordell said that this engine would reduce costs and would be far more efficient than the diesel engine. Mr. Lionel Forsyth, president of Dosco, made this statement:
I believe that the only way to find out whether it is the real answer to the motive problem is to build it, and try it on the rails.
He went on to say that if they wanted to they could have done that that year, in 1955. Well, this year we are voting $50,000 towards the project compared with $110,000 the year before. We either should not be voting a cent or we should be voting enough to clean it up and get it over with. Let us stop this horsing around with this thing. Nothing has been more poorly handled than this particular project which offers such tremendous possibilities to eastern Canada, Alberta and other sections which are interested in coal. We do not know yet whether or not it is going to work but here you have the president of Dosco saying, "Put it on the rails and try it out." Here you have the man to whom we have been paying the money, a man in whom we apparently have confidence, the man who has done a great deal in developing it, one of Canada's eminent scientists, saying that it is the most superior form of motive power yet developed and that it is going to be the solution to the problem of the coal industry and everything else.
Perhaps we are holding it back deliberately until all the diesels become outmoded so that the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. will not have to write them off too quickly. There must be some explanation for the delay. The hon. member for Bow River referred to another experiment a few moments ago. My information, and frankly I get it from the general manager in Dosco in Cape Breton, is that in Great Britain they have an engine, perhaps produced by a different approach-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: They had one 50 years ago and 30 years ago in the United States.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
-and they have one in the United States. They are convinced they have solved the problem. Whether we have made the right approach I do not know. The minister says our approach is better. I hope that is so, but let us stop approaching and let us get there because there is something radically wrong with our approach when something so vital to the country as this is has been allowed to dilly-dally as long as it has. We see now that this year the proposed expenditure is reduced by 50 per cent. I am not urging increased expenditures on an over-all basis or anything of that kind, but I do say that either this expenditure should be cut out entirely or we should put
6, 1956	5731
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys all our resources back of it and get it over with. I suggest, with all due respect to Professor Mordell, that we take the experiment out of the university laboratory. Let us get some commercial engineering firm and give them a contract so that with Professor Mordell's assistance and with all the money necessary they may try it out and bring it to a conclusion one way or the other so that we will know whether we have something here that may be of tremendous importance both to our transportation systems, because they need efficient transportation, and also to the coal industry.
I hope that the minister will reconsider this matter and will put his emphasis behind it. I am quite sure that this committee and parliament will be very glad to vote additional moneys if they are necessary, and they obviously are. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I only rise at this time because the member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings paraphrased rather badly what I had to say last year. Four years ago I went down and had a look at the experiment. The minister was good enough to organize a delegation of members to go down and have a look at it. I was interested in it because the press, in my judgment a bad source of information, were playing up this experiment as the solution of the problem of the coal industry of Canada. It was the miracle that was going to put coal in competition with natural gas, oil and all the rest of it. It was going to revolutionize our transportation system, particularly the railways. I wanted to go down and look at this thing because I had heard a lot of talk about it and had read about it. So along with the minister and members of the House of Commons I went down and looked it over. The coal-fired gas turbine engine is not a new thing. They had that type of engine 50 years ago in a locomotive in Britain but it did not work. They had it 30 years ago in the United States and it did not work. The difficulty always has been to find a cooling system that will prevent the burning off of the blades of the engine. They could not find a solution and they abandoned the idea a long time ago. What Professor Mordell is working on now is not a new type of engine. What he is trying to find is a cooling system that will enable the blades of the engine to stand up to the terrific heat.
At the time when I came back I did not say what was put on the record by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings. I said that as far as that engine going to save the
5732	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys coal industry was concerned, it was at least 10 years away from any commercial use. I might say that in discussing this matter with the president of the C.N.R. in committee on several occasions, I made that statement and he said that in his judgment I was a realist, that it was not going to perform overnight the miracles that the press would lead you to believe. My concern was that I wanted something done to assist the coal industry rather than pin our hopes on something that might or might not help. It certainly would not solve the problem. At far as saving Alberta's coal industry is concerned, there is not any to save. It is fairly well gone. That is equally true of the British Columbia industry. Those industries are gone. The coal industry is gone in the west but it has been replaced by oil and gas. Quite a chunk of the Nova Scotia industry is also gone beyond repair. The thing we want to understand is that we do not want to keep on having false hopes on the question of saving the coal industry.
I went into this question fully last night and I expressed the opinion that the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. are dieselizing the railways from coast to coast. They are making an investment that it will take at least 10 years to write off. At the present time they are dieselizing the railways in Newfoundland. That is their program and they are going ahead with it.
It was stated on several occasions that this engine is interchangeable with the present diesel units, and that you could instal this type of engine with the present diesel unit. You cannot do that. I found that out fairly definitely. I also found out that before they can adapt that engine to a locomotive, the C.N.R. will have to send in some of their engineers and technicians to work on that experiment and build a locomotive to which that type of engine is adaptable. What does that add up to? First, you must get the C.N.R. interested to the point where they are going to come in and work on it.
With respect to asking the minister to solve the problem, may I say that he is not an engineer. He knows about as much about it as I do. He had a look at it, and you are obliged to depend on what people tell you. But if there is a solution for the coal industry in this particular experiment, why is not the coal industry sufficiently interested? The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings says the president of the coal company, Mr. Forsyth, said: Get it on the rails and get it running. If it means that much to that corporation, why are they not contributing to the experiment? Why have they not some engineers working on it? They have engineers, and good ones. Why are they not
[Mr. Gillis.l

putting some money into the thing? If that industry is going to benefit to the extent suggested by the press and others, then they should be "in there pitching" and trying to find a solution.
As I said last night, I do not believe in keeping my head in the sand. I want to get done for the industry something that is going to mean something to it. I said last night that in my judgment, after looking at the engine, I figured that it would perhaps be an excellent marine engine if they can find what Professor Mordell is looking for, or it would be an excellent engine by means of which to generate power for small power plants. But even if it were installed on the C.N.R., if it were to perform so as to affect the economies in fuel which they say it will effect, it is not going to use much coal, and it still is not much of a solution for the coal industry.
I do not know what is going on in the United States although I have seen some reports in the press. But if they have perfected that engine to the point where they can operate it in a locomotive, why are we wasting time in searching? Why do we not get the information from there and put it to use instead of spending money on an experiment of our own? I think that would be the logical thing to do. However, as I said, I do not know any more than what I have seen in the press as to what is going on in the United States. Nevertheless, I know this. Unless there is a big development in thermal power-and I think that is one of the solutions for the coal industry-there is not much hope.
I have never objected to this grant. We have spent $650,000 so far on the experiment. I have said right along that it is justified on the ground of being a grant to McGill University so as to enable engineering students to sit in there and study and work on that proposition. There were quite a few of them around there the day we were looking at it.
I think it would not be a bad idea if the minister had another pilgrimage and took down there a group of members from this house who are interested and had another look at it, talked to Professor Mordell and found out from him directly when this engine might be of some commercial use, and what the possibilities are of getting the co-operation of the C.N.R. and of industry that is going to benefit financially and from an engineering standpoint. With the interest that has now been created, I think another trip down there would result in bringing back to this house some concrete information that would prevent in the future any speculation or the posing of hypothetical questions that cannot be answered.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have left the matter of the coal industry to this very item. I know it certainly is not the solution to the condition in which the coal industry finds itself today. However, it is a program which, if successful, anticipates the large consumption of coal. I cannot agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South that an embargo on coal is the solution. In western Canada, particularly in British Columbia, we have in the United States a large market for coal and coal products. Our coke and other by-products of coal are being shipped in large quantities to the western states. Then again much of the other product of the mining industry finds a market in the United States. If an embargo were to be imposed on coal in eastern Canada, it follows that there would be some sanctions against our products in western Canada.
I have been interested in this Mordell experiment since first coming to Ottawa in 1949 and I have followed it fairly closely. I believe the problem now is that in the heat exchangers corrosion is taking place owing to sulphur in the fuel itself. It is not a serious problem and it is different entirely from that suggested by the hon. member for Cape Breton South in that it is not corrosion of the blades of the turbine. There is no corrosion to the blades as the gas flowing through the turbine is pure air. The heat exchanger through which the burning gas is driven certainly is the place that takes the strain from the burning of the gases. When it has been determined that a proper alloy can be fabricated for the lining of the tubes in the heat exchanger, I believe the problem will be pretty well solved.
One only has to stand opposite or ride in an aeroplane such as the North Star to realize the wear and tear from vibration that is the consequence of that type of motor. Then, if one rides in a Viscount, which has a turbine type of motor, one realizes the very great advantage of the turbine engine for this use or any other. Even now the railroads are finding the maintenance of diesel locomotives quite a large factor in their operating costs. I understand that they are having considerable difficulty with the pistons. Anyone who knows anything about mechanics realizes that the very high compression, which is part of diesel locomotion, results in a great deal of wear and tear and vibration which is not one of the factors of a turbine motor. In every respect, therefore, the turbine is a much more efficient operation.
I believe that we are overlooking a particularly significant development here and that we should put more money not only into the development of the coal-fired gas turbine, 67509-364
6, 1956	5733
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys but in the processing of coal for other purposes. Sitting on the research committee for this past session, I have found that we are spending many millions of dollars in research into other aspects of industry. Specifically, we are spending millions of dollars for the development of atomic energy for peaceful purposes. I think that other plans and developments are being dwarfed by this great desire to rush into the development of atomic energy, while we are allowing other more simplified fuel elements to go by the board. The fuel element in an atomic reactor is a very expensive product. It requires large mining operations, great milling operations, and then the cost only begins to materialize after having gone through those processes. Coal may be obtained on the surface in many places in Canada simply by going in with great shovels and stripping the overburden. Coal has been the lifeblood of the nation for many years, and may well be in the future. We know that we have coal reserves for up to a thousand years at the present rate of consumption.
It is, therefore, my belief that having regard to all those factors and the particular benefits of turbine motors as opposed to internal combustion motors, the coal industry itself and the people who work in that industry, instead of voting $50,000 this year we should be voting something over a million dollars. Apparently, this $50,000 is all that is required at the present time to complete this very limited experiment that is taking place at McGill University. When one visits the installation there one has the feeling that they are actually hampered, in a sense, by the lack of interest and the inadequacy of funds which are provided for this purpose. They go for many months unable to carry out a certain experiment because some particular plant does not seem able to supply them with the necessary implements. It seems to me we are not providing sufficient funds for the experiment itself. I feel that we should appropriate more money for this particular experiment, and certainly for other experiments in the use of coal.

The hon. member was not here yesterday. Perhaps he does not know that the Minister of Finance has also asked for a supplementary estimate of $50,000 for this project which will carry the program through until the end of this year. This project has never been held up for want of money. Professor Mordell would be the first to tell him that.

As the minister knows, this is one of the largest oil deposits in the world. I think the estimate is about 200 billion barrels. It could happen in the event of war that we in this country would also find ourselves in an exceedingly embarrassing position so far as oil supplies are concerned if something is not done.
I know that in the west we have been doing a tremendous amount of development in the drilling of oil wells and we are producing a rather large quantity of oil and I suppose that amount will be increased as time goes on; but I doubt very much that we will ever get to the point in western Canada where we could supply from drilled wells all of the needs of Canada and the North American continent in the event of an emergency, although we could do that very easily if we developed the proper method of extracting oil from the Athabasca tar sands.

the provincial government in Alberta has been making rapid progress in the development of the extraction of oil from the tar sands and I think they are working closely in co-operation with some of the large oil companies. The most important problem seems to be the treatment of the bitumen and the resulting oil which must be treated in order to permit it to flow through a pipe line, and then breaking it down into its various components and removing the sulphur. To that end we are undertaking experiments at the mines branch. It is a high-pressure experiment. We have had great difficulty getting high-pressure vessels which are necessary for the experiment. The basic purpose of the geophysical year is a study of the earth's upper atmosphere and the manner in which it is influenced by the sun's radiation. Practical applications include radio communications, meteorology, high altitude military projectiles and a better understanding of the earth's immediate environment.
In co-operation with the Department of Transport, national research council and the Department of National Defence, the dominion observatory is equipping and operating ten to fourteen magnetic stations in Canada extending along magnetic meridians from Resolute Bay-latitude approximately 75-to southern Canada. The Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is providing the instruments while some of the stations are being manned by other departments. The observations are all to be collected and arrangements made for their analysis and publication by the dominion observatory.
As well as the projects I have mentioned, important additions are being made to our northern seismographic station at Resolute Bay. Systematic observations of sunspots, flares and other disturbances on the sun are being made at Ottawa throughout the geophysical year. In co-operation with the departments I have mentioned, observations are being made of the aurora, the ionosphere and of meteoric phenomena at Ottawa, Agin-court, Meanook, Newbrook, Victoria, Yellowknife, Baker Lake and Resolute Bay.
In presenting the estimates for the operation of the dominion coal board in this fiscal year I am pleased to report that there has been an improvement in the coal situation over the last twelve months.
This improvement is demonstrated in increased production of Canadian coal from
14.770.000	tons in the fiscal year 1954-55 to
15.014.000	tons in the fiscal year just ended; in an increase in the consumption of coal of over 2 million tons and in a reduction of the subvention payments of some $773,171. I may add that this reduction in the amount of assistance did not result from any appreciable decrease in the tonnage of Canadian coal moved under subvention assistance but from the reduced cost of assistance per ton from $3.07 last year to $2.92 in the year just ended.
In the province of Nova Scotia output was down by almost 100,000 tons. This was not due to lack of markets but rather to the closing of a high cost operation. The mechanization of the Sydney collieries began to show concrete results during the year. Cost of production is dropping and the output per man day is slowly climbing upward. During the year a market opened up for Nova Scotia coal in the United Kingdom and the continent.
[Mr. Prudham.l

In the fiscal year some 230,000 tons moved to Britain at a cost in subvention of approximately $494,000 or $2.14 per net ton.
Shipments to Quebec and Ontario were slightly lower than in the previous twelve months but this was due more to difficulties in transportation and delivery than to any lack of markets.
The Nova Scotia producers have been working to develop new methods of burning coal. One new product, the dominion down draft furnace, has received an award of a certificate of merit from the national design centre and is finding an increasing sale in the maritimes. This radically new furnace for household use is at present being offered in Ontario and Quebec and a growing market is hoped for. The Department of National Defence has installed a number of these furnaces in the new Gagetown project where they are being fully tested over a full year's operation. My colleague tells me that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has also been testing out this equipment.
Turning to New Brunswick, the output of coal at 880,000 tons is not only 100,000 tons more than last year but forms an all-time record for the Minto field. Increasing tonnages of this coal are being used for the production of electricity and for industrial use. In Saskatchewan also production of 2,302,000 tons constituted a record. This coal finds a ready and increasing market in the industrial and electrical power fields.
Alberta has been the most depressed section of the Canadian coal industry but this past year has seen at least a slowing up in that trend, although I am not trying to minimize the seriousness of the situation in Alberta. The bituminous mines in this area have been largely dependent on the railway market. The switch to diesel locomotives and to oil burning steam engines continued, causing some further loss of markets. This loss was not nearly as heavy, however, as in the previous year. The cold winter in western Canada, together with the increased wheat traffic, threw a considerable burden upon the railways and the fuel requirements were considerably heavier. Steam locomotives scheduled for retirement were needed for operations and, while locomotive coal consumption was down by some 300,000 tons, the unexpected need for more fuel found the coal stock piles depleted and caused an unexpectedly heavy demand for supply from the mines. The cold weather also increased the demand for household coal and the subbituminous mines have enjoyed a relatively prosperous year. Altogether, Alberta fiscal year production of 4,621,000 tons is somewhat higher than the 4,591,000 tons in the 12 months previous.

Finally, the British Columbia mines show some increase in output from 1,344,000 tons last year to 1,460,000 tons in the 12 months ended March 31, 1956. This increase, however, is due to the improved operations in the Crowsnest pass area while the Vancouver island mines do not show any increase.
The coming year will undoubtedly produce some difficulties. The Alberta bituminous mines will continue to lose more of the railway market while the domestic producers will be affected, of course, by the vagaries of the weather. There will be an increase in the consumption of western coals for power production when new plants now under construction come into operation.
The amount of money required for subvention purposes shows a substantial decrease. The estimated amount of $9,210,250 is $789,750 below the estimate of last year and some $1,356,623 below the actual expenditure of last year. This reduction in amount does not mean any curtailment in the assistance offered to Canadian coal. The amounts provided on specific movements in the various orders in council remain exactly as in the previous year. The subvention payments have always been calculated as the amounts necessary to enable Canadian coals to meet the competitive laid-down costs of imported coals in the designated markets. Over the past 12 months there have been substantial increases in the laid-down costs of imported coals as well as some decreases in the cost of Canadian coals. These mean that, while it required $3.07 per ton to move the subvention coal in 1954-55 and $2.92 in 1955-56, it is estimated that it will require $2.46 per ton to move approximately the same tonnage in 1956-57, assuming that there is a movement of 3,700,000 tons. I am glad to repeat that, while part of this has been due to increased cost of imported coal, a substantial part has also been due to the increasing efficiency of Canadian coal production resulting in lower costs.
It is hoped that the improvement noted in the Nova Scotia coal picture over the last 12 months will continue through the coming year. The hon. member for Cape Breton South has mentioned that they are doing a good job there in lowering their production costs. The increasing effect of mechanization will be reflected by greater efficiency of operation and higher output per man day. That has been the trend in the early part of this year. It is estimated that the amount of money parliament is being asked to provide for subvention assistance and the existing orders in council defining and regulating the payments will enable the Nova Scotia
6, 1956	5739
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys coal mines to find outlets for their production in the year ending March 31, 1957.
I should like to refer to the delivery of coal to Newfoundland, which has been mentioned by some hon. members. There have been recurring difficulties in this delivery arising partly out of the seasonal availability of schooners and in part out of the lesser number of these vessels engaged in the trade. A meeting was held in Sydney in January of this year of those interested in this movement, with the chairman of the dominion coal board in the chair. A very full and detailed review was made of the difficulties and the possible remedies. I understand that as a result there has been a marked improvement in the loading of the vessels and that basic investigations are being carried out by private interests looking towards the development of better means of transportation over the longer term.
Liquid fuels are expected to continue to take over new domestic outlets as well as to win some established customers from coal. There will possibly be some gain to coal from wood consumers but not enough to overcome the loss to other fuels. When we read that there were in Canada in 1951 some 1,436,050 homes in which coal was the principal fuel while in 1955 there were only 1,115,000 in this category, it gives us some picture of the loss. At the same time, oil burning installations increased from 774,535 to 1,656,000 homes.
Of course this is not the whole picture. The demands for coal for industrial use continue to grow and this trend no doubt will continue. While most of this growth is in Ontario and Quebec, where United States coal is the main supply, the growing demand for electricity in the coal-producing provinces is providing an expanding outlet. Reports by the power companies to the dominion bureau of statistics estimate increases in the installation of fuel electric stations in the mari-times from 324,000 kilowatts in 1954 to
513,000	kilowatts in 1958 and in the western provinces from 605,000 in 1954 to 1,058,000 in 1958. This shift in markets, as I remarked on a previous occasion, will create problems for many of the existing producers.
Present reports indicate that the United States coal trade will be hampered by a shortage of cars during the year and that costs will be somewhat higher. This trend should help to provide outlets for Nova Scotia coal but, unfortunately, cannot be of much assistance to western Canada.
The hon. member for Bow River and the hon. member for Macleod have suggested that we should block off a portion of the Canadian market for Canadian coal. It is a very nice idea and I would be all for it if it were possible to do it but I do not think it is.

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys One difficulty is that most of the industrial installations in Ontario are built to burn United States coal and Alberta cannot supply the type that these plants are equipped to burn. Another problem and difficulty in moving western coal in large quantities to industrial Ontario is the fact that as a rule Alberta coal does not store well, and it has to be delivered as it is consumed. Actually I think that the solution to the coal problem and the problem of the communities situated in the Crowsnest area and other coal-producing areas in Alberta is to encourage industry to locate in those areas. The provincial government and the federal government should both give all the encouragement possible to the solving of that problem.
I know that the industries, the mine companies concerned, are extremely active in trying to diversify their operations. There is one very healthy coal operation in the Crowsnest pass. They have a diversified operation. They have coke ovens. They have the largest supply of coking coal west of the Mississippi. They have lumbering operations. They are engaged in oil development. Another company is endeavouring to develop base metal deposits in the area. I know they have shipped samples of the ore to Europe for experiments on extraction. Although it is far from proven that they will get good results from their efforts, I know that they are spending a great deal of money and are endeavouring to establish another industry which will provide stability not only for the coal industry itself but for the communities in that area. I believe that is the positive approach. I do not think that putting restrictions on imports is a positive approach to the problem even if it could be carried out under our constitution. The hon. member for Cape Breton South last night I think pointed out that this government has not the power to dictate what type of fuel shall be used in any particular area. If anybody has the power, it is the provincial governments concerned. I do not think that the answer to the coal industry's problem lies in that direction.

Mr. Chairman, this item of the coal board is one which probably embraces as many people and affects their lives as much as does any other one item in the whole estimates of our parliament. It is a matter on which some of us-and I know I have done so-have spoken at length at other times, and I do not propose to do it now.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South spoke last night with respect to this matter


and of course he represents thousands of people who are employed in this industry and who are directly affected by it. In order to show its ramifications I need only say that in my own constituency, which is removed some considerable distance from the actual coal fields themselves, we too are greatly affected by this matter because it is one of the principal markets for agricultural products in the maritime provinces. As the coal industry prospers and develops, so do the farmers of the Annapolis valley, and of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island generally. As the coal miners suffer depression, so do our farmers suffer from loss of markets and reduced prices. They are perhaps not as directly affected by it but they are affected by it and to the same degree as are the people living within a few miles of the coal mines themselves. That is why this is an item which is important to all of us, because I am sure the same situation applies in the province of Alberta and in the province of British Columbia or wherever else coal may be mined. It is not only the miners themselves but those in the other associated industries who are affected by the large number of people who at one time were employed in this industry and who unfortunately have suffered from greatly reduced employment during the past few years.
I am not one who wants to cry blue ruin over this matter. I remember that this is not the first time the coal industry has suffered a marked depression. I am sure the hon. member for Cape Breton South and I myself remember the situation 25 years ago when, in the island of Cape Breton, there was mass unemployment, there were labour difficulties and there was actual starvation and it looked as though the coal industry was through. People said that the coal industry could never recover from the depression of those days. Yet a marked recovery was obtained. The government of R. B. Bennett, working in co-operation with the provincial government of Nova Scotia, by increasing subventions and carrying out an aggressive marketing policy, went a long way towards restoring prosperity in the mining areas of Cape Breton and therefore of Nova Scotia generally.
Then again during the last few years we have been faced with technological changes which have threatened the very existence of this industry once more. A few moments ago the minister pointed out the greatly reduced sale for coal because of the dieselization of the railways. In 1953 or 1954 the Canadian National Railways purchased 700,000 tons of coal. Some people suggest that by 1957 or 1958 these purchases will have virtually disappeared. The St. Lawrence basin, which
;uly
at one time presented and offered a great market for Nova Scotia coal, is threatened by the development of the St. Lawrence seaway and the prospect of American coal being brought down by water carrier into that area. Then there is the development of the gas industry which also is going to cut substantially into the market for coal.
I was interested in what the minister said about the development of this domestic furnace to which he referred and in connection with which he said a citation had been awarded to the company for producing it. I think this could be said, perhaps not in criticism but as a statement of fact, and I think the coal operators will be the first ones to admit it. In the days gone by they did not worry too much about marketing. Certainly they did not worry at all about the domestic consumer. They had the demands of the railways. They had the demands of heavy industry. They would meet your orders if they saw fit to do so but the local customer, the domestic consumer, was the forgotten man. If he did not want to take the type of coal, the size of coal and the dirt which they had to offer, it was just too bad for him; he could freeze. That was virtually the attitude which they took. Then suddenly, because of these changes, the industrial market and the railway market have been substantially lost to the coal producers. Now they are struggling desperately to meet the demands of the domestic consumer and to satisfy him.
We now have this down-draft furnace which was produced two years ago, which is on sale, and which apparently is a tremendous improvement over the old coal-burning furnaces. If that same aggressive attitude had been adopted 10 years ago by the companies concerned, they would now be enjoying a much greater proportion of the domestic market than that which they now enjoy. Of course, once having turned to oil, the domestic consumer is not going to throw out the oil furnace and put in a coal-burning furnace, although perhaps it is comparable in efficiency and cost with the oil furnace. Hence they have much responsibility for the way in which they have lost these markets, particularly domestically. It is encouraging to see that they realize that now

I think they frankly admit it-and that they are going to combine efficiency and production together with aggressiveness in sales and are going to attempt to meet the demand of the customer rather than ignore him as hitherto has been the case.
One would not worry too much about the coal industry, or rather one would worry about it but one would face its problem and 67509-365

I recall what happened in the Studebaker plant, I think it was, many years ago. They were the largest producers of carriages in the world. However, the horse and buggy passed. The automobile came to the fore.
I do not think the coal industry is going to pass. I think it has a substantial basis in the economy of this country and that over a period of years it will recover. In fact the report of the dominion coal board says that while the current situation, viewed as a whole, is cause for grave concern, it is to be remembered that the Canadian coal industry is basic and one upon which our economy is still largely dependent.
I think that is a fundamental statement, Mr. Chairman. It is because of that we say this government does have a responsibility in helping to assist this industry in every way possible, not just to keep it in the horse-and-buggy era, but to carry it through a trying period of transition. The reports of the minister's own fuel board suggest that within a decade the costs of other fuels will be increased, the industrial potential of this country will have been developed and there will be an increasing demand for coal. The coal industry must then be in existence to meet that demand. As was suggested this morning, I think by the hon. member for Cape Breton South when referring to the gas turbine engine, perhaps by the time we have that development the coal industry will have passed out of existence; that is the danger, Mr. Chairman.
It is different from operating a grocery store or some sort of a retail business where you can shut the doors, pull down the blinds and have it closed for one year or 10 years. Then you can come back, sweep out the cobwebs, and go into operation. Once these mines are allowed to close, once the shafts fill with water, once the men are taken out, the difficulty and cost of reclaiming them would make it virtually an impossible situation. The mines, having gone, cannot be reclaimed. As I said, therefore, it is essential that this government, in co-operation with provincial governments and in co-operation with the industry itself, do everything possible to maintain the coal industry during these days.
5742	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
I think we have failed in this parliament and in this government in the development of a truly national fuel policy. I think that is the basic problem. One day we have emphasized the place of gas and a great deal of money is spent in assisting the gas industry. We have control now of certain rivers in connection with the production of electricity so as to preserve power for Canada. All those things are desirable and all those things may be necessary, but there is no over-all co-ordination; there is no development of a fuel policy as such. I think that is one responsibility of this government and one in which this department has failed.
There was a reference last year to the interdepartmental committee on energy, and that was to be a committee composed of representatives from the various departments of government which would meet and work out a national fuel policy. What do we find? Look at the report of the coal board and you find that the interdepartmental committee met twice. Look at the preceding board report and you find the committee met twice during that year. There were four meetings in two years, Mr. Chairman, and that is not a very aggressive way in which to develop a national fuel policy.
I think that more must be done in that connection than has been done before. I agree with the minister that probably greater industrialization may be the solution to the oroblem. Undoubtedly, there is going to be greater industrialization. Even in the Atlantic provinces there has been a great increase in industrial development, but not nearly as much as in the central provinces. Some criticisms have been levelled at this government by maritime members because it has done very little to assist in the development of industries in these provinces, particularly those industries associated with national defence where direct government control would have permitted much more to be done than has been done. As those industries are developed, so will the market for coal develop.
I want to pay a word of respect to certain industries such as the Nova Scotia Light and Power, for instance, to which reference has been made before. They have installed greater units this year for the burning of coal in the development of electricity. I think there again there has been lack of co-ordination in the past. I am sure that in my own province probably too much money has been spent in the costly development of hydro-electric energy by trying to get the last bit of power development from relatively small water courses. If more attention had been paid to the development of


electrical energy from coal we might have been in a much better position than we are today. At least Nova Scotia Light and Power, by installing this new unit, is providing a certain market for Nova Scotia coal, and as similar installations take place in various areas in the maritimes, so will the consumption of coal increase.
The emphasis has been placed, I think, on the development of these other sources of power. I feel this government is justified in doing more for the coal industry than it has before. A few minutes ago the minister said that, apparently owing to a little increased cost in maritime coal and an increased efficiency in the production of our coal, the amount paid out for subventions per ton will be a little bit less this year. That is a very fortunate situation, and as we develop increased markets in our own country that can continue. Until that situation arrives this government is justified in spending, for subventions and assistance in the movement of coal, more money than it has heretofore.
We had a situation last year where the Canadian National Railways complained about the quality of the coal and refused to buy it on a certain basis. As a result, our government had to pay several million dollars additional to the Canadian National in order to have a certain basis for our coal. Those expenditures are just, because when you spend hundreds of millions of dollars in the development of a seaway, when you advance hundreds of millions of dollars for the building of a gas line-justified as those expenditures may or may not be from a national standpoint, and we are not criticizing that for a moment-then this department and this minister are more than justified in spending the money available to the coal industry, even more money than has been spent in the past. This industry must be kept together during this period of transition.
We have the new problem of freight rates. Freight rates have been increased, as we know, by an interim order of the board. There are going to be further hearings this' fall and we will know then what the final increase in freight rates will be. The government has in the past assisted in meeting those increased costs. I know the hon. member for Cape Breton South raised the question yesterday, and it has been raised before. I hope that this afternoon, in dealing with this particular item of subventions on coal, the minister will tell us what the policy of the government is with respect to meeting these increased costs to the coal producer because increased freight rates just came into effect during the last few years.

As I said, the ultimate problem is the greater industrialization of the country and that is perhaps a place where this government and the provincial government can co-operate. Next week there is to be a meeting of the provincial premiers of the maritime provinces called by Premier Flemming of New Brunswick, in which they are to consider the whole basic problem of the maritime economy. As a result of this conference certain recommendations will be made to this government. The Prime Minister has said he would welcome those recommendations and they would receive direct consideration. We hope that is true. This is one of the basic problems of the maritime economy, this matter of coal production and coal mining. It is essential to the economy of at least two provinces in so far as the Cape Breton area is concerned, the Cape Breton population and those farmers in Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia. The New Brunswick farmers, of course, do not come directly into contact with the Cape Breton area but there has been a development in the coal mining industry which has been helpful to that province.
There is some reason, therefore, not perhaps for optimism, but determination that this industry will be kept at least at its present standard of employment, which is low enough, lower than it should be. It must at least be held there during this interregnum until the situation develops which is envisaged by the minister's department when it says that in 1965 there will be a situation in this country by which the coal industry will again be utilized to its full extent.

Mr. Chairman, you will remember that last evening when I was speaking I was called to order, and I did not complete what I had to say. I am not going to repeat anything I said last night. I might say that I agree with everything that was said this afternoon by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings. As he very well pointed out, this question affects not only the coal miner of Nova Scotia, it affects the whole economy of Nova Scotia. If the industry goes down the province pretty well goes down with it. That is why I have been so vociferous on the matter ever since I came into this house.
Last evening the picture I was trying to leave with the committee was that in so far as actual knowledge of the future of coal, or of any other fuel in Canada, is concerned, there is not very much known. Most of our information comes from the press. I put on the record last night statements from different sections of the press that were directly opposite to each other. One statement painted a picture of the golden era of coal; coal was 67509-365i
6, 1956	5743
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys going to begin to come into its own. The next statement threw it down flat, wrote it off, and it was pretty hard to pinpoint the problem accurately.
I said last night, as the minister indicated this afternoon, that the dominion government did not have the authority to bring this problem to a final conclusion and find a solution because actually the problem is one that, under the British North America Act, rests with the provinces and to a large extent with the operators of the industry. The Dominion Coal Board Act was assented to on July 17, 1947. The powers and authority of the board were clearly set out in the act. The powers and authority given to that board at that time were based on the condition of the industry at that time. Drastic changes have taken place in the whole fuel set-up of Canada in the last nine years. Problems have been created that are interprovincial or company and provincial, and the federal government cannot move to meet them under their present powers.
What I wanted to say last night in summing up what I had said was that I believe what is needed in this country today is an expansion of the Dominion Coal Board Act to give the board the necessary authority to bring some sanity into the production and distribution of fuel in this country. In addition to having its powers broadened the board should have on its membership personnel from the oil industry and the gas industry. The coal industry is represented there at the present time. It should include someone who has some knowledge of the potential of atomic energy, because that is around the corner.
If the situation in the fuel industry is allowed to continue as it has been in the last few years one type of fuel will destroy the other. Nobody can tell with any degree of accuracy what the economic value of natural gas will be in Quebec. The men who are going to pipe that gas down east cannot tell you; neither can the government of Alberta, because when the line comes into Quebec, before they can sell gas or fix a price for it they have to deal with the public utilities board of the province, which will fix the rate. Nobody knows what it will be. Heating systems should not be changed until the price is known. I am reasonably sure that whether it is oil or gas they swing to they will find it will cost more than coal. Many of the small industries in this province that changed over to oil not so long ago are switching back to coal because of the cost.
If we allow the coal industry to drift as it has been drifting, in the next 10 years there will be no industry to rehabilitate. Whether or not you want coal you will not be able to
5744	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys get it. As the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings said, you cannot reclaim a coal mine. You close a mine down. It is closed for a year or two. You are not going to open it again.
There is another thing. It will take you at least five or six years to qualify a miner underground. He has to write examinations. I want to warn the committee that once a miner with five or six years' experience comes above ground he will not go back again if he can find employment somewhere else. I am convinced, after looking at the thermopower development, for example, in Alberta at Battle River, that that is one angle we should be promoting in the maritime provinces. A very good job is being done in Alberta, but they have much cheaper fuel.
In the final analysis I say this government, in co-operation with the provinces, should expand the act and increase the powers of the board. The kind of personnel that I suggest should be placed on the board with the end in view of making an examination of the different zones in Canada as to the fuel that is most economic in a particular zone. That should be done before it is too late. If you had men of the calibre I have in mind from the different fuel industries who could consult together and examine the economies in the different zones across Canada, there is no doubt in my mind but that coal from Cape Breton island would be allocated to the province of Quebec. It is the logical fuel for that area. Regardless of anything else I believe there is a market for at least 5 million or 6 million tons of coal in that particular area for many years to come; but somebody has to take the responsibility for making that kind of survey.
I do not think there is anyone in a position to do that but the federal government, with a board that is pretty competent in the whole field of fuel. The present coal board has a lot of information, a lot of data and many trained personnel today that they did not have in 1947. It would not be very hard to expand the board if it had the power to go into the problems which arise out of the question of the proper economic fields for the different fuels. I think you have to do that if for no other reason than to prevent one fuel killing the other because of the greed and grab for markets at any price until they get in there. Once they get in there, of course, they root the other fuel out. The heating plants are adapted and you pay their price or you do not have any heat.
I think it is a bad thing to give a monopoly to oil, gas or any other fuel in any section of the country and have that section of the country completely dependent on it. The
[Mr. Gillis.l

only logical and sensible answer is a national fuel policy with that kind of board administering it, and with the power to regulate and allocate as far as fuels are concerned.
Toward the end of last session I moved a motion in the house having to do with this particular question, and I was supported by the whole opposition. The Ontario press is pretty careful in going out on a limb on anything that is new. The Globe and Mail had editorials saying that this was a sensible idea. In view of the present situation in the country in the field of fuel, we may be spending millions and millions of dollars on hydro, on oil, on natural gas and on coal. But don't forget what the British are doing right now on atomic energy. In a few years' time because of that development-maybe in the United States and definitely in Britain-we are going to have to work along similar lines, and we are just throwing money away because we do not have any authoritative body in this country that is making a competent study of the whole question of fuels now and in the future, and it is very nearly time we did. The framework of the act is here now, and it is just a matter of giving it a little consideration and expanding it.
The minister did tell us last year that this interdepartmental committee was working. Well, they had a couple of meetings, but there is no doubt there may be some smaller body that is actually doing the research and the digging and we have not received the benefit of it. Perhaps the minister is closer than I am aware to doing the kind of thing I am talking about. Perhaps they are ready to set it up, but it has to be done under an amendment to this act.
I do not want you to call me to order again, Mr. Chairman, but I just wanted to say this in order to complete what I was saying last night. . I hope the minister's department will soon get around to bringing some sanity to the whole question of fuels.

Mr. Chairman, I think the minister and perhaps all the committee will readily understand my interest in this matter when I indicate that almost 25 per cent of all the coal mined in Canada, or about one-fifth of our national production, is mined in my own constituency of Moose Mountain. The coal industry in my province is in very excellent condition. In spite of the fact that western coal production has gone down almost 30 per cent in the last ten years, we are happy to know that in the lignite fields of Estevan we have more than held our own. In 1955 we produced 2,239,000 tons of coal with a sale value of $4,250,000. It is therefore quite important to my province and to me in particular, representing the constituency I do, that everything be done to promote the industry and maintain it in a healthy state.
I was extremely interested in the remarks made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South and the hon. member for Digby-An-napolis-Kings. I want to join with them in suggesting that the time is long overdue for this government to take the responsibility of setting up a national fuel board by which both the conservation and utilization of our fuels can be handled in an intelligent manner.
As I listened to the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings I noticed he pointed out that in his view some of the things that are wrong in the situation existing in the coal mining industry in his area are going to be corrected, but it has taken a long time for the department concerned to take the proper action, and this indicated that something is being done in the way of setting up a national fuel board.
I remember reading speeches made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South prior to my coming to the house in 1945. Even that long ago the hon. member was pointing out to the government of that day that in Canada we should have a co-ordinated board under the control of this government, which would have the interests of the various types of fuel producers in mind, to set up a program which would be conducive to the

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys development of the various fuels on a sensible basis. It is well understood that in the last few years across the country we have had a tremendous development in alternate fuels. In my own constituency we have perhaps one of the largest oil fields on the North American continent. Not only do we have an estimated reserve of 13 billion tons of coal, or perhaps 24 per cent of all Canadian reserves, but we also have some of the greatest potential oil fields on this continent.
I think the point made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South and the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings was well taken, that we should have a policy under which there would be no friction between the various ways to utilize our fuels. It is all very well for the minister to get up and say he feels that the best interests of the various fuel industries, speaking about coal in particular, can be served by locating industry in those areas, but it may be that without a plan industry will be set up where competitive fuels will come in and the industry will not be in a competitive position. I think the point made by the hon. members I mentioned was extremely well taken.
This afternoon I want to point out in particular my own concern over the production of coal in my constituency. Over the past ten years we have developed perhaps the highest type of specialized coal mining to be found anywhere in the world, but despite this fact a situation could arise whereby that industry would find itself in great competitive difficulty. Lignite coal moving to the city of Winnipeg and western Ontario markets today furnishes power for some large pulp and paper mills but the new rulings of the transport board, the interim horizontal freight rate increases, might put that industry in an uncompetitive state and perhaps will have a bearing on the future of the coal industry in my constituency. I should like the assurance of the minister after I resume my seat that the government has taken into consideration the situation which has evolved through these interim horizontal increases in freight rates.
I wish to point out to the committee that as far back as 1914 the transport board agreed that, due to the fact that lignite coal was not competitive with bituminous coal, there should be a 10 per cent differential in freight rates. Estevan coal, for example, moving into the Winnipeg market in 1914 was $1.80 a ton; bituminous coal at that time was $2 a ton. Under the present rates and increases subsequent to 1914, lignite coal moves at a freight rate of $3.30 a ton as compared with $3.50 a ton for bituminous
