Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a short statement at this time. As hon. members know, no new legislation has been introduced this session having to do with veterans affairs, with the exception of a minor amendment to the Veterans Business and Professional Loans Act, which comes under the Department of Finance.
This does not mean that the government and officials of my department consider that further amendments to the legislation making up the veterans' charter may not be necessary in the future. As I have mentioned in previous years, that legislation is under constant review with the intent that the charter must meet the changing needs and requirements of the veteran and his dependents.
It must be agreed, however, I submit, that great progress has been made in the legislative field during the last five years. In 1951 substantial amendments were brought down to the Pension Act, which came into force on January 1, 1952, and the act was again amended in 1954. The War Veterans' Allowance Act was amended in 1952 and again last year. Part II and part III were added to the Veterans' Land Act during the 195354 session, and the Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act was passed in
1953.	A complete consolidation of the treatment regulations was effected during the year
1954,	and these regulations have been amended several times since during 1954, 1955 and this year.
Writing in the October, 1955, issue of The Legionary, the Legion publication, Very Rev. Dean John D. Anderson, then dominion president of the Canadian Legion, said:
Today the task of obtaining adequate legislation is almost complete. True there are areas where improvements could still be made and will be made. But by and large the legislation picture is gratifying.
As hon. members know, the dominion convention of the Canadian Legion in session last month in Vancouver passed a number of resolutions concerned with proposed legislative amendments, and as soon as these recommendations are received by the government I can assure the committee they will receive the careful and thorough consideration of the government and the officials of my department. Here I wish to pay tribute to the
Supply-Veterans Affairs Canadian Legion, the national council of veterans' associations in Canada and the other veterans' organizations which have done so much to promote the well-being of the veteran and his dependents in our country. The efforts of these organizations and their willingness at all times to co-operate with the Department of Veterans Affairs are reflected in the legislation we call the veterans' charter of which all Canadians are, I believe, justifiably proud.
As hon. members know, the most significant changes made in the War Veterans' Allowance Act last year were in the rates and ceilings, the former being increased by 20 per cent to $60 monthly for single persons and $108 for those on married rates, and the ceilings being raised to $840 per year for recipients at the single rate and to $1,440 for those receiving the married rate. As of March 31, 1956, there were 51,781 recipients on war veterans allowance with an annual liability of $40,207,916. These recipients included 38,427 veterans of all wars, 13,208 widows and 146 orphans.
There has been a marked increase in the number of applications for war veterans allowance since April 1, 1955, the date the amendments to the act became effective. In the year ended March 31, 1954 there were 5,545 new applications approved for war veterans allowance and in the next fiscal year ended March 31, 1955, there were 6,322 such applications. In the last fiscal year ended March 31, 1956, 8,562 new applications were approved.
As announced in the house last session, the rules under which grants from the assistance fund could be approved were reviewed and the formula extended to include allowances for clothing and other personal items. In the fiscal year ended March 31, 1955, 5,681 veterans and widows received assistance from the fund, and in the year ended March 31, 1956, the number was 6,256.
While generally speaking the assistance fund has been meeting the purpose for which it was set up, I have recently asked the appropriate officials in the department to review its administration and application with the intent of perhaps again widening the formula to help some of those war veterans allowance recipients who cannot supplement their incomes through casual earnings. Veterans in receipt of the allowance are also eligible for free treatment for any condition, and the cost of that treatment in the 1955-56 fiscal year was estimated at about $13 million, which was almost one-third of our total treatment cost.
The administrative wrinkles in connection with the putting into operation of the new rules regarding casual earnings, including the

As hon. members know, part III of the new act provides for additional loans to farmers and small holders at the time they are settled. Up to the end of March, 1956, 1,387 farmers, 3,422 small holders and 22 commercial fishermen had been granted these additional loans under part III. We are closely watching the operation of these two new parts of the Veterans' Land Act to make sure they are meeting the purposes and objectives which parliament intended when the amendments were made to the Veterans' Land Act in the 1953-54 session.
It is interesting to note that the 10-year period has expired for a number of veterans, and as of July 1, 1956, 2,830 veterans have now earned their conditional grants. As many veterans were settled in 1946 and 1947, we anticipate that several thousand veterans will earn their conditional grants during the next 18 months. I think all members of the committee will agree that the Veterans' Land Act has been a most successful rehabilitation measure.
The Pension Act, of course, remains one of the main pillars of the veterans' charter. At the end of May, 1956, there were 194,035


persons in receipt of pensions under the act, with a total annual liability of $128,685,908. During the last five years, or even during the last 10 years, one trend which is very evident is the constant decline in the ranks of world war I pensioners, both veterans and dependents, and the steady rise in the number of world war II pensioners. As I informed the Legion convention at Vancouver, the Canadian pension commission has completed several reviews during the last two years, undertaken as part of the policy of ensuring that the maximum benefits of the Pension Act are made available to veterans, and this committee may be interested in some of the results.
These reviews were carried out in conjunction with the regular work of the commission, and in co-operation with the treatment services branch of the department. One of these was a review of all world war I pensioners whose disabilities were assessed at 40 per cent and 45 per cent. As hon. members know, these awards were stabilized if they had been in effect for three years or more, but we were of the opinion that a medical re-examination would disclose an increase in disability in many instances.
The chairman of the commission, Brigadier J. L. Melville, issued orders accordingly and over 3,000 such pensioners were reexamined. As a result a very substantial number of these awards were increased to 50 per cent or more, making their dependents eligible for an award in the event of death.
Similarly, a review was undertaken of all awards to world war I veterans for defective hearing, which awards had also been stabilized. Over 6,000 reviews were arranged and it was found that there had been a further deterioration in hearing acuity in more than half of these pensioners. This additional loss has been compensated for by a corresponding increase in their awards.
At the beginning of 1955 a more liberal policy in respect to awards to dependent parents was placed in effect, and a review commenced of all such awards in payment. It was felt that these recipients were entitled to similar consideration, respecting allowable income, as were recipients of war veterans allowance and old age assistance. The total allowable income for one dependent parent is now $85 monthly, except for widowed mothers who may have $95, and $120 per month for two dependent parents.
In the two-year period since the enactment of the amendment to the Pension Act which provided for the payment of additional pension for legally adopted children, additional pension has been awarded on behalf of nearly

3,200 adopted children, a much larger number, I must say, than was originally anticipated.
Since the passing of the Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act, 679 children of those who gave their lives for our country have been approved for educational assistance. The students are enrolled in nursing, teaching, engineering, business administration, law, medicine and many other courses. We are convinced there will be substantial increases in the numbers of students approved for assistance under the act during the next few years, as most of the eligible children are still in secondary or even primary school at this time.
Under the veterans' treatment regulations the department provides treatment, hospitalization and domiciliary care for veterans and for other authorized persons under certain circumstances. This, of course, is one of the most important aspects of the work of the department. The cost of our treatment services last year amounted to $45,381,181, including hospital construction in the amount of $3,465,177.
The amendments to section 13 of the treatment regulations last year-this is the section with the sliding scale of charges designed to protect the veteran against hospitalization costs which might ruin him financially-came into effect on August 1, 1955. During the last fiscal year 6,359 patients were treated under section 13 at a cost of $2,356,563.90. Of this amount only $546,726.61 was charged to the patients, which I believe shows the effectiveness of the sliding scale.
Here I should like to mention the fact that the Department of Veterans Affairs suffered a severe loss last December in the untimely death of Dr. Wilfred Parsons Warner, who occupied the post of director general of treatment services for the last 10 years. Hon. members will recall that Dr. Warner had been responsible for the setting up of our hospitalization system throughout Canada in the Department of Veterans Affairs. I know he will be remembered by veterans for his professional qualifications, for his human and down to earth approach to their problems, and for the success he attained in providing veterans with the best possible care and medical treatment available anywhere.
The department has been fortunate to obtain the services of Dr. John Crawford, formerly with the Royal Canadian Medical Corps at the Department of National Defence. He is the new head of treatment services. He brings to veterans' affairs sound professional qualifications, with a good background of administrative experience.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
As hon. members know, 100 years ago Queen Victoria authorized a medal to be made from the metal of the guns which had been captured at Balaclava and to be awarded for valour in the presence of the enemy. It was known as the Victoria Cross. This year, during the week commencing June 25, the centenary celebration of the award of the first Victoria Cross took place in London, Canada being represented by a large group of V.C.'s and relatives, of whom two are members of this house.
Under arrangements made by the Canadian V.C. centenary committee and with the cooperation of T.C.A. and various shipping companies, a total of 118 persons were provided with transportation to the United Kingdom by air and sea at public expense.
The V.C.'s, who included two still serving in the army, numbered 36. They were accompanied by 37 relatives, and there were also 44 relatives of posthumous and deceased V.C.'s. Although I have not as yet received an official report, I am informed that the ceremonies were most impressive and the arrangements for the Canadian party in England extremely well handled by the staff of the D.V.A. office in London, England, and the officers of the Canadian joint staff, national defence, to whom my appreciation is extended. I feel that all of us will be honoured by the prominent part played by Canadian V.C.'s and their relatives in this unique celebration.
Before taking my seat, Mr. Chairman, I should like to mention the national memorial and cenotaph which, as I announced in the house some weeks ago, will be built on Nepean point overlooking the Ottawa river. As I said in the house, the world war II Book of Remembrance and any similar books which may be prepared in the future, as well as a copy of the world war I Book of Remembrance, will be housed in this national memorial. The matter is now in the hands of my colleague the Minister of Public Works, and I understand that the architects are presently engaged in preparing the plans and specifications.
The annual report of the Department of Veterans Affairs has been edited and it is now in the hands of the queen's printer. Full statistical information regarding the administration of the department will, as usual, be found in that report. I, of course, will be glad to give all the information I have to members of this committee on any aspect of the work of the department, either under this item or subsequent items.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we appreciate the remarks of the minister and his comprehensive report of the veterans affairs department. May I, at the outset, join with him in expressing the appreciation which I know the people of Canada feel for the attendance of our V.C.'s at the centennial celebration in England, and particularly the two who represented us from this House of Commons.
The minister truly said that there has been no legislation this year emanating from the veterans affairs department. I was pleased to hear him say this does not mean that the department does not realize there are amendments which should and must be made to the different veterans' acts. When we review the estimates, Mr. Chairman, we realize there has been very little change in the department during the last year. As a matter of fact the estimates for last year, 1955-56, were $245,808,151 and for 1956-57 they are practically the same, $245,413,819. This shows that there has been very little change in the veterans department.
The minister mentioned the fact that the veterans' charter is the basis of veterans' legislation. We who have been here for many years, since 1945, realize that the veterans' charter did contain some very comprehensive legislation covering the needs of veterans. We also realize that in these changing times there must be changes in veterans' legislation. I remember that in those days the veterans' committee was the busiest committee in the House of Commons. This was true not only in 1945, 1946 and 1947, but right through until that legislation was completed. Then again during the Korean war we were fairly busy bringing legislation up to date to see that the veterans of Korea received the same benefits as the veterans of world war I and world war II.
There is a feeling amongst some veterans, Mr. Chairman

possibly it is not justified- that now there is no war the government believes there is little need to attend to veterans' problems. I think this idea gains ground from the fact that at the present time we have a minister who is sharing his activities with the Post Office Department. In previous debates this year this matter has been brought before the house, and it was before the Legion's convention in Vancouver. I think it is generally felt that the veterans would like to see a full-time minister on the job.
There are so many ramifications to veterans' problems. We only have to listen to the minister's report this afternoon to realize the many problems facing the veterans department and the minister. There are 

homes for veterans, farms, businesses, insurance, fisheries, pensions, war veterans' allowances, hospitalization and many more that I could mention. I do not believe there is any department of government that has to deal more with human problems and the human element than has the veterans affairs department. Even the health department is not concerned with these problems to the same extent. In the field of health there are health departments in the different provincial governments and the municipalities. Veterans affairs is an exclusive problem of the federal government.
We feel there should be a full-time minister. I might say that anything which might be considered as neglect of this department- and I do not say there has been neglect, particularly-but anything which would make the veterans feel this department was not as important as other departments, gives them serious worry. The veterans of this country are very jealous indeed of their Department of Veterans Affairs. I do hope this is the last session of parliament in which we shall see a part-time minister dealing with this most important department. In addition, the Post Office Department is a very important department. I could name other departments of government in which I do not think the ministers are very busy or need to be very busy. If the work in these two departments which should be done by the minister of a department is to be done, a minister should be on the job full time in each department.
The minister spoke about the possibility of new legislation. There is no question in my mind, Mr. Chairman, that the many acts which he mentioned this afternoon do require amendment; there is no doubt in my mind or in the minds of veterans across Canada that there are many problems and many things concerning veterans which must be considered and brought up to date. I think we can show, for instance, that there has been considerable unfinished business. When I say "unfinished business", Mr. Chairman, my mind goes back to the different meetings of the veterans affairs committee in this House of Commons, when matters were repeatedly brought before the committee and the government having to do with amendments which should be made to certain acts, particularly the War Veterans' Allowance Act.
I should like to deal with that for just a few minutes. I shall deal with it under the head of unfinished business as far as the department is concerned. I was very pleased to note, and not surprised in the least, that at the convention of the Canadian Legion in Vancouver a short time ago some of these problems were again brought to the attention of the country

by resolutions presented to the convention. I might say in passing, as has often been said in this house, that I suppose one of the finest pieces of veterans' legislation that has ever been presented to any parliament was the war veterans' allowance legislation that was presented to this parliament in 1930. The history of that legislation has been given a great many times, and it is not necessary to repeat it this afternoon.
I should like first to mention the ceiling on the war veterans' allowance. This is not new, Mr. Chairman; it is something which has been discussed at every veterans' meeting we have had in the past five or six years. As the minister pointed out, the ceiling on income for single veterans is $840; the ceiling on income for the married veteran is $1,440. The minister and other members, particularly the members of the veterans' committee, will recall that the recommendation which was made in 1952, I think it was, and repeated again in 1955, was that the ceiling should be $1,200 for single veterans and $2,000 for married veterans.
This was recommended to the committee after very serious study by Legion committees all across Canada. It was a great disappointment to veterans all across Canada when the government did not see fit at that time to raise the ceiling. It has worked a great hardship on many individuals who are recipients of war veterans' allowances.
As far as the employable veteran is concerned, it was argued that the ceilings were high enough because under the present ruling regarding casual earnings the veteran who is employable can earn an extra $600 a year; also, under section 4 of the act a veteran during months of employment could earn whatever was possible for him to obtain. So far as the employable veteran was concerned the ceiling did not mean very much. The very fact that the department increased the allowable casual earnings, and the very fact that we have section 4 of the act, were a recognition that more money was necessary as far as the unemployable veteran was concerned. The unemployable veteran, the man who has nothing but his war veterans' allowance or perhaps a small pension, is placed in a very serious position.
I want to emphasize this afternoon that one of the first things to which the Department of Veterans Affairs should give attention is this matter of increasing the ceiling on the war veterans' allowance. For instance, take the veteran who has reached the age of 70 years. If he has no other income but his war veterans' allowance, owing to the ceiling he can obtain only part of his war veterans' allowance because he is also a recipient of the old
Supply-Veterans Affairs age pension. If he is single he can receive a total of only $820 a year. Then there is the disability pensioner. These things are not new. I know hon. members have heard them discussed in the veterans' committee. We brought in amendments and pressed for these considerations in 1952 and 1955.
The disability pensioner with a small pension of $25 or $30 a month is also prejudiced against. If he is a single man he cannot receive more than $840 a year; if he is married he cannot receive more than $1,200 a year. Take a man who has worked hard during his life and at the time of retirement has a small superannuation allowance which he has earned. If he receives $25 or $30 a month as superannuation allowance he is prejudiced under the present ceiling of the War Veterans' Allowance Act. Of course we have been told that there is an assistance fund. Well, the assistance fund amounts to $10 a month and is given only to those who have absolutely nothing except their war veterans' allowance. If they are in receipt of $60 a month they may obtain another $10, bringing the amount up to $70 a month. If one is to judge from the amount of money which has been paid out by the department, very few people are receiving any substantial amount from the assistance fund.
As far as the employable veteran is concerned, he is not going to be employable for very many more years. He is employable today because his health is good. These men of the first world war are old men today. The average age of the war veterans of the first war is in the vicinity of 66 or 67 years. In a few years these men who are today earning extra money will not be able to earn that money. The numbers of unemployable veterans are increasing every day of every month. I do hope this matter will receive very careful consideration at the next session of parliament.
Something else which was brought up at the Legion convention at Vancouver which hon. members have been mentioning for many years was this question of granting the war veterans' allowance to men of the first war who had service only in England. I have always felt that these men were entitled to consideration. I think that entitlement is emphasized today more than at any other time. These are old men. Many of them served in England because they had no choice; perhaps they were good at training men in the reserve areas. Perhaps they were men who either worked at headquarters in London or at some particular job which did not permit them to go to France. Spending four years of army life away from home was not easy on them. While the original idea
5752	HOUSE OF
Supply-Veterans Affairs of the war veterans' allowance was to give it to men who had served in the front lines in the trenches-and that is the reason these men have been denied it-that idea has been altogether changed as far as the war veterans allowance is concerned.
I would like to point this out as well. The mere fact that a veteran set foot in France qualifies him for consideration for the war veterans' allowance. Perhaps he arrived there in 1918 in the very last month of the war and perhaps he did not get within miles of the trenches; but nevertheless that man is entitled to consideration for war veterans' allowance. But the man who spent four hard years in England frequently working under very trying conditions is not entitled to consideration.
To emphasize again how the original idea changed regarding service in the trenches, I would point out that men can receive the war veterans' allowance today if they have had dual service. That means they may have simply arrived in England during the latter days of the war and never gone to France and served in Canada here during the second world war. Such a man is entitled to war veterans' allowance but, as I say, the man who had four years of hard service in England does not receive any consideration.
When this matter was up before, the question of the time of arrival in England was mentioned in the committee. We know there were thousands of men who arrived in England for training just about the time the war ended. I think perhaps an amendment might very well take into consideration the fact that the man who had gone over in 1914, 1915 or 1916 and who had long service there should be entitled to consideration, but not the man who arrived in England just a short time before the end of hostilities.
The matter of the cost was mentioned in the 1955 committee. At that time we were told that it would cost an estimated $9 million. That estimate seems very high to me. The minister told us today there are 51,000 recipients of war veterans' allowance. That figure includes men of the first war, men of the second war, men of the South African war, men of the northwest rebellion and all the widows and other dependents. I suppose the men who served would total approximately 30,000 all told. Out of that 30,000 probably 25,000 are veterans of the first war. I think the 11,000 who were mentioned as those who would be entitled as recipients of the allowance for service in England if an amendent were made is a figure that is out of all proportion. I think it is an exaggeration and should be carefully reviewed once more. As I said before, many


of them are men who arrived in England just as the war was ending. This is a matter which I feel should and must be considered. These men feel a great injustice is being done to them, and I share that view.
At every veterans' committee we have had during the past ten years we have had a group of very nice old ladies visit the committee, and they have always presented an interesting brief. I refer to the widows of our allied veterans, the non-pensioned veterans' widows. A veteran who did not serve with the Canadian forces but who served with one of our allied forces and who lived for 20 years in Canada was qualified in the same way as our own veterans to receive the war veterans' allowance, but he had to reside 20 years in Canada. If he qualified, his widow would automatically receive the war veterans' allowance at his death.
Many of these allied veterans lived in Canada for almost the required 20 years- 18 or 19 years, and sometimes within a few months of the 20 years-and then died and their widows received nothing. These ladies who visit us, as I said, have made application time after time that they be considered for pensions if they themselves-as widows of allied veterans who had every qualification except 20 years' residence-have resided in Canada for 20 years. I think that is a reasonable request. I am sure this house will be surprised to learn that the total estimated cost presented to us in this regard is between $300,000 and $400,000; there are about 700 of them, according to the evidence we have had.
Here again is something that should be taken into consideration when the War Veterans' Allowance Act is amended, in justice to these women. As the evidence before our committee last year revealed they are dying off very quickly, and there would not be any great burden on this country even if their number were increasing, in view of the small amount of money required to take care of them.
I believe there should be a review of the Pension Act; it should be brought up to date. I hope at the next sitting of this house a veterans' committee will be set up which can review our Pension Act to see if the pensions we are paying are at all in line with the cost of living as it has changed from year to year.
When the minister was speaking he mentioned the cost of dependent parents. I am pleased that this matter is receiving consideration, because I have always felt it was a great injustice that we did not give consideration to pensions for dependent parents at the time we increased the pensions for widows from $75 to $100. If a dependent parent lives with a widow who is receiving the $100 a month and if that widow has children the

parent can receive only $40 a month. If the widow marries and the dependent parent has to seek a home somewhere else, she still receives only $40 a month. This has created a hardship for many dependent parents, and I am sure if it were properly adjusted it would not cost this country very much.
The minister has referred to hospital treatment. When the Legion met in Vancouver there were present veterans from the United States. At the present time a pensioner living in Canada receives hospitalization which is more or less satisfactory, but if a Canadian soldier living in the United States requires hospitalization he receives it for his disability alone. As the minister has said, these men are getting older all the time and the disabilities which they suffer bring on other disabilities. They are men of 65, 67 and 70 years of age.
The representatives of Canadian veterans living in the United States asked for a new reciprocal deal for the Canadian veteran living in the United States and also in Great Britain or other countries. They asked that when hospitalization was required it be paid for by the Canadian government, and that a reciprocal arrangement be made whereby the United States veteran living in Canada would receive hospitalization here when required.
This comes under section 13 of the treatment regulations. In the information sent out by the department entitled "Should Illness Strike" there is this sentence:
This treatment is available to veterans in Canada only.
The words "in Canada only" are emphasized. There are some 35,000 Canadian veterans living in the United States, a small proportion of whom are pensioners. The spokesman for this group at Vancouver was Mr. Wright, who said:
The Canadian ex-serviceman below the border is entitled under the present act only to his disability allowance.
He was referring to hospitalization for disability only.
He forgoes everything else. If he can't afford to travel back to Canada when he is sick, then he must pay the shot where he is.
This is something we could very well take under consideration. While these men are living in the United States, they served in the Canadian army just the same as those who are living in Canada, and received their wounds in the same battles.
There is another matter with which I do not intend to deal at any length at this time, as it can be discussed when the items are before us. I refer to the need of homes for older veterans, a matter which I have brought up before. This is an increasing problem, and
Supply-Veterans Affairs I note that the department realizes this because on page 15 of the departmental report the following appears:
General welfare needs of older veterans are increasing in importance and volume, and a sustained effort is required in helping them with their problems. More world war I veterans are becoming retired or able to do only light employment, entailing increasing calls on the department's statutory provisions for assisted maintenance, and co-ordinated search by the staff for suitable work.
The whole point is that the day is fast coming when these men will no longer be able to look after themselves, and I am referring now not only to veterans but to all older people. This is becoming a serious problem in this country and homes for older people should be established all across the country. Not long ago I read an article in the Saturday Evening Post dealing with nursing homes in the United States to which older people were farmed out and left to await death. In countries like Great Britain, Sweden and many others, provision is being made for older people. With the provinces, the municipalities, the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Department of Veterans Affairs working in conjunction something along this general line should be done for our veterans and our older people.
On April 27 I asked the minister a question regarding the protective staff of the house, and he promised that he would give a reply later on. I asked whether military service applied in connection with seniority.

speechtext:
Perhaps I was away. I will check on it. I was pleased to hear the minister pay his tribute to the Canadian veterans' organizations. We have always felt in our committees and in the house that the organizations he mentioned, the Canadian Legion, the national council of veterans and others, have given great service to war veterans all across this country. As a matter of fact I was greatly interested in an editorial in a recent issue of The Legionary. The editorial is headed, "Legion Principles", and I should like to read one part with which I agree 100 per cent.
They have by their ceaseless efforts sought to secure just recognition of the hard-won rights of their disabled comrades, of the widows and dependents of those who made the supreme sacrifice. These will always be their first responsibility. They have sought justice for those who have become prematurely aged by the exposures and privations of war. They will continue their efforts on behalf of these gallant men who, having saved-their countrymen from oppression and slavery, only ask for a modest allowance sufficient to maintain themselves as self-respecting citizens.
I think that sizes up the situation as far as the efforts of the different veterans' organizations are concerned. I could make a comparison, Mr. Chairman, and perhaps it is not out of place to do so. I remember that after the first great war there were thousands of veterans in the United States who marched on Washington and demanded a $10,000 bonus. Recently we have seen them again asking for enormous amounts of money. I should like to refer to an editorial in the Christian Science Monitor of June 12, 1956.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Applewhaite).]

It mentions the bill the veterans are trying to get through congress and has this to say:
This bill would grant within two months of enactment a monthly pension of $105 to any veteran of the two world wars or of Korea who has reached the age of 65 and whose income, if married, is less than $2,700 or, if single, less than $1,400. The criterion is reaching 65, not wounds, sickness, or accident suffered during military service.
The editorial goes on to say that if the bill should pass it would mean a cost in excess of $400 billion to the American people in the next 44 years. I simply mention this to contrast the difference so far as the Canadian veteran is concerned. I am not saying this in disparagement of the United States veterans, but we all know that Canadian veterans of the first world war served for four years in France while many United States veterans did not serve in France for more than a few months. Our Canadian veterans, under the leadership of the different veterans' organizations, have never at any time been unreasonable in their requests to the country or the government. Neither the Canadian Legion nor the other organization has ever made excessive demands upon the people of Canada. I believe the demands to which I have referred this afternoon are very modest. I believe they are demands which could and should be given consideration by the Department of Veterans Affairs.
I was pleased to hear the minister mention some of his officials, particularly Dr. Warner. We know what splendid service he gave. I should also like to refer to Brigadier Topp, formerly of the Canadian pension commission but now retired from that position. I am sure all veterans valued the great service Brigadier Topp gave to veterans before his retirement. I am not going to impose upon the committee any longer. I have been granted extra time, but I will have time to discuss many other matters later. I wish to thank the committee for their courtesy.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to join with the minister in his reference to the loss the department suffered in the passing of Dr. Warner. I was one member of the house who was privileged to do considerable work with him from time to time and to go to him to find the solution to certain problems. I join with the minister in his expression of the loss that has been suffered. Anyone who took an active part in trying to iron out problems with reference to treatment particularly found a very active friend in Dr. Warner, and I think the veterans' hospitals across Canada, which compare with any hosiptals in the country, will stand as a monument to his memory. I trust that the man who has taken
JULY e, 1956
his place will be able to fill his shoes. He has been set a pretty hard task.
I listened with interest to the minister's report, and I want to compliment the department for the things they did without any urging or any pressure. It indicates to me at least that whether or not we are pushing the department, there seems to be a constant review within the department and the pension commission so far as pensions and the welfare of veterans generally are concerned. The fact that without any solicitation, as far as I know, the 40 per cent to 45 per cent cases were re-examined and adjusted to 50 per cent by the commission is to me a thoughtful and generous gesture on their part, because not only does it give the veteran the additional income but it also protects his wife and family in the event that he passes on.
I want the minister to know that as one member who is interested in the commission I appreciate that gesture very much. I believe that the fact that there was a reexamination of 3,000 cases in certain categories and that they were stepped up to the 50 per cent mark represents a pretty fair assessment on the part of the commission, and I think they should be complimented for it. As an opposition member I believe in shoving them when I have to, but also in giving credit where credit is due.
The minister mentioned another item for which I think we should express our appreciation. He referred to the fact that 3,200 adopted children have been brought under the act for pension purposes. That not only serves the purpose of giving the children some security, but also serves the purpose of encouraging veterans who are pensioners and in a position to adopt children to do so and give these children homes. I know many institutions across this country which have the responsibility of caring for unfortunate children will appreciate this gesture on the part of the minister. I think that is a problem that was crying for a solution for some considerable time. I am glad to see that-again without very much urging or pushing-the department or commission saw fit to make that adjustment.
Another matter under the minister's department, according to his report, that I thought was encouraging was the educational assistance made available just a couple of years ago to veterans' children in certain categories. The fact that 609 children were able to take advantage of that legislation shows that it was needed. As time goes on I think more and more use will be made of it. I just wanted to say that in appreciation of what the commission and the department have done during the time since the last veterans' affairs committee met.
Supply-Veterans Affairs On this matter of the minister occupying the dual position of Minister of Veterans Affairs and Postmaster General, may I say this. I received one letter on the question. Of course it represented a command within my own area. My answer to that letter was that I did not think the fact that the minister was obliged to make an announcement in the house occasionally on behalf of the Post Office Department-one that was handed to him by the deputy postmaster general, who runs the department anyway-had detracted very much from the minister's performance of his duty as Minister of Veterans Affairs. I do not think it involved a great deal of work because, as I have observed it during the time I have been here, that is about the situation. But I do not think that the minister should continue to be obliged to accept that responsibility. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration does a very good job in that field, and he had the portfolio for some time. In order to remove any thought on the part of the veterans that the minister is occupied fully by the Post Office Department, I suggest that the department should be handed over to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext: Thank you very much.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext:
The reason I say that is this. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and the deputy postmaster general are old friends. They occupied the same office for a long time. They both live in Ottawa. I am sure you get along with him much better than does the Minister of Veterans Affairs. I just want to say that I never considered that matter too seriously, because I fully realize just how much work there is involved in making these announcements. As to the people who have complained, that is all I have heard. Of course if I thought the dual position in fact detracted in any way from the minister's handling of his own department, I would be one of the first to complain.
There are a few odds and ends which I think still require cleaning up. One is the matter of casual earnings. I believe the department should give serious consideration to lifting that ceiling. I believe that the demand of the Legion for $2,000 for the married recipient of war veterans' allowance and $1,400 for the single person is reasonable. We have the fact that the basic amount is set at $108 plus $12 in certain cases bringing the allowance up to $120. Lifting the ceiling on permissible earnings does not mean that it is going to cost any more. It is not going to cost the government any more. However, it will provide an incentive for the recipient of the allowance to go out and try to earn something.

Supply-Veterans Affairs I think that particular point should be given serious consideration by the minister's department.
The second sore spot, in my opinion-and it is becoming more apparent as time goes on- is the discrimination that exists in the war veterans' allowance as between the man in the second war and the man in the first war. A veteran of the second war, because England was declared a theatre of war in certain circumstances, can qualify for veterans' allowance. The veteran of the first war cannot do so. As has been pointed out time and time again, I think you are safe in saying that at least 90 per cent of the men of the first war who stayed in England did so because they were ordered to stay there. They were cooks, technicians and people who went into the pay and records offices. They were instructors and that kind of thing. They were under orders to stay there. I know many of them who wanted to go over to the front and who broke their hearts to leave their units.
These people did not suffer the hardships of the trenches, and they were not wounded. People of that calibre came back, and they were people who had either a profession or a trade; they had training of some kind. They were people who could come back and find a job in this country, with a reasonable degree of health, and they have been employed. Now they are getting along to the age of 65 and maybe to 70 but they are not old enough for that $40 a month and they still cannot qualify for war veterans' allowance.
I think it is time something was done for them. As the hon. member for Royal said, even if you took them on now, you are not going to have them very long. Many of them are getting around to the point where they are not going to be here much longer. The situation is a piece of discrimination. I know I am getting a good deal of correspondence on the matter now, and it is only within the last few years that I began to get it. It arises because of the fact that they have been moved off jobs because they have reached the retiring age, many of them in industries and what have you that do not have any pension schemes, and they just go out with nothing. I receive some rather pathetic letters from them.
Looking at that age group again and the question of establishing homes for them, may I say this. I do not know what the situation is in the rest of the country, but I know that in Halifax, at Camp Hill hospital, there is an annex that is designed for that purpose. I have looked it over. I know many of the people there. The Red Cross maintains an institution close by where meals and recreational facilities are available at very low cost
[Mr. Gill is.i
in comparison with what you must pay in the city. During my last visit there I found the men to be quite happy and contented. They have at their disposal a nurse who stays there with them. There is a doctor who comes in there and takes care of them. Some of them are placed two in a room. Others have a room to themselves. I did not hear any complaints.
That is the situation around Camp Hill in Nova Scotia. I do not know what happens in the rest of the country. I think the veterans will have to stay together. They want to be together. You cannot farm them out into the regular old people's homes. They have something in common. They want to reminisce about their experiences. When there is a group of them together they are quite happy and they can keep occupied. They do a great deal of work there making handbags and bracelets. They can pick up the odd bit of change in that way. Of course that is the situation at that one point, but I assume it is just about the same across the country. I trust the minister will give serious consideration to changing the act to include veterans of the first war for war veterans' allowance purposes.
Another pet complaint that I have had for some time is with respect to the imperial veterans' widows. As to the imperial veteran who had 20 years' residence in this country and passed away, his widow can qualify for war veterans' allowance. Even with respect to a veteran of the Italian army in the first war living in this country who passes away after 20 years' residence, his wife can qualify for war veterans' allowance. But the imperial veterans' widow who finds herself in the position that her husband passed away perhaps six months or a year before he completed the 20 years' residence qualification finds she cannot qualify for the pension.
There are not very many who are affected by this. I know there are two women living close together, both of whom came to this country at about the same time, and one widow gets the pension while the other does not. I think that distinction should be removed. The fact that a man lived in Canada, worked in Canada for perhaps 18 or 19 years, paid taxes in Canada, established a home in Canada and died in Canada surely should be sufficient qualification. He was not out of the country.
I think when that clause was inserted in the first place it was designed to be used in the case of people who came here for four or five years and then went back for three or four years. However, when the residence has been continuous until the time of the man's death, I think the widow should

qualify. It is a very sore point in my part of the country. I know it is in my riding, because we had a lot of imperial veterans who came to that part of the country after the first war.
Another matter I hope the minister has in mind, because it involves national defence and veterans affairs, is the matter of unemployment insurance for men in the service. During the last committee meeting the Legion recommended that we should give consideration to bringing service personnel under the Unemployment Insurance Act on a contributory basis, just like any other employee in industry.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext: That is national defence.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext:
That is right, but it has to be handled by both departments. I have talked to the Minister of National Defence about it twice. His department was going to conduct a survey to ascertain if the men in the service wanted to come under unemployment insurance. I do not think that is the proper approach. If you went out and conducted a survey in any industry as to whether the employees wanted to contribute something, they would say no.
I think it is up to the Department of National Defence, with some urging from the Department of Veterans Affairs, to bring this about for a lot of people who enter the service and who do not know where their best interests lie. They sign up for three years or five years, perhaps intending to srtay and make a career of it. Some men going into the service today leave jobs, and there is no civil reinstatement act applicable when they come out. They are unemployed.
Some of them still think the old system prevails, just as it did for the veterans of world war II and Korea. Those fellows got unemployment insurance and these fellows think they should get it, too. I know, because I meet quite a few of them. I tell them if they went into the service after a certain date they are not covered.
The service is going to be a career. It is employment for some of these people and I think they should be protected against unemployment when they come out. In the defence debate I pointed out to the minister that the wastage from the services during the one year 1955 equalled the number that was taken in. What they call wastage are those people who are weeded out, people who cannot qualify. They cannot meet the standards but they are kept in perhaps two, three or four months or a year and then weeded out. The number going out in 1955 equalled the number coming in, and that is quite a large group of men. Most of these fel-
Supply-Veterans Affairs lows would not find employment for some time, and they are not protected by unemployment insurance. I think the approach your department should make to national defence is that if you are going to canvass the services and ask the men if they want to contribute something, the answer will be no.
If this government, after due consideration and a proper analysis of the problem based on statistics, determined that it was in their best interests to protect them, then laws would be passed. There will not be much fault found with them. I know I would not have very much trouble convincing a group of boys in the services today, who are not thinking very much about anything but having a good time-I did the same thing at their age.-that it would be in their best interests to have this. It would only cost a few cents a day, so knock off a few glasses of beer. I know national defence is thinking about it, and I trust the minister will also lend his weight to it.
There is something I said at one committee meeting and I have talked about it several times since, but I want to mention it now. Are the service bureaux across Canada adequately staffed? Within the last year or so we were unfortunate enough to lose the chief pensions advocate at Halifax. He dropped dead as the result of a heart attack. A Mr. C. P. Coleman took his place, and I believe he is a very good man and doing a very good job. He has not been there long. I have had considerable correspondence with him. I have met him, and I think he is an excellent person. I believe the man he replaced went out very quickly because of the stress and strain, the long hours of meticulous work examining these files, assessing evidence, preparing new files, checking forms and trying to get doctors' reports. It entails burning a lot of midnight oil.
They have staffs to help them a little bit, but I do not consider they are adequate. I believe men like Coleman at Halifax, who handles all the Nova Scotia problems, should at least have another top flight man with him. I believe there is plenty of work for two men. We have all seen cases where the commission is blamed for delays, but I believe in fact the point of delay has been in the service bureau office because it was not able to handle the volume of work. I think the minister's department should take a square look at the staffs in the bureau offices to ascertain if they have all the personnel they need.
I have another problem here which is an old, outstanding one. It is one about which perhaps very few people have heard. When
5758	HOUSE OF
Supply-Veterans Affairs the pensions investigators were set up after the first war, they were classified as such and paid a certain salary. When the department was streamlined they established welfare offices and welfare officers. The old pensions investigator was reclassified and designed as a pensions visitor. There are only 15 of them left in Canada and they are all getting along toward retirement age. Last year their salary was brought up to that of a grade 4 stenographer, and then it was increased by $300. This still leaves them receiving $800 per year less than their co-workers who are classified as welfare officers.
What is bothering these people is that for many years they did the welfare officers' work the hard way. They worked out of central offices and covered the province by dog team, horse and buggy or motor car where they could. They went from house to house visiting these claimants. Today the welfare offices are on a district basis. The field men do not go out to any great extent. These old pensions investigators would be on the road for months at a time without getting home. The welfare officer living in the district is home at least every night.
I think they are completely justified in asking to be reclassified into the same category as the welfare officer. That differential of $800 in pay should be made up, because it would mean much to them in their superannuation when they reach the age of retirement. Only 15 people are involved in the whole of Canada. To relieve the anxiety that exists in the minds of those 15 people, and the uncertainty of their future with respect to superannuation, the department should give some consideration to ironing out the problem.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we in this group would join the minister and others in expressing regret at the loss of Dr. Warner. I am satisfied that if the minister has been able to find a suitable successor in Dr. Crawford he is indeed fortunate because specialists are scarce and particularly hard to find. He is to be complimented on his choice.
So far as the group who went to the centennial celebration of the establishment of the Victoria Cross is concerned, we would rejoice in the thought that those who received the reward posthumously were represented by relatives or friends of their families.
I would agree that this department is particularly difficult to administer because it does have a humanitarian aspect and that, of course, calls for a recognition of the sentimental as well as a realistic view of the obligation we have to the men and women who are being served by the administration.
I am sure we all realize it is difficult at times to decide whether a case is one of merit or


whether it should be denied. It makes me often wonder whether one can legislate for humanitarianism.
It is therefore with a great deal of joy that I am able to tell the minister that I am very happy over the co-operation I have had from the department, from the minister, his officials, his parliamentary assistant and others. I think this department is one that has captured the spirit of the government and of the administration, which in this case happens to be to assist rather than to resist those for whom they are trying to work. I feel the minister is to be congratulated on the job he is doing. If he can handle both portfolios of which he is now in charge as well as he has been handling the one department of which he has been in charge in the past, I am satisfied that no one in this country should suffer because of his administering those two departments.
My reason for making these remarks, Mr. Chairman, is an incident that took place during the recess. During that time it was my task to draw to the minister's attention, or to the attention of his officials and his deputy, Mr. Garneau, the case of Mr. Frederick J. Hards, who was suffering from sclerosis. He, his wife and three children had to live entirely on a family allowance cheque which amounted to something like $15 a month. He is a war veteran of the second world war. This young man and his family were suffering, and it was drawn to my attention. The legion branch in New Westminster and other interested bodies immediately got in touch with the minister's office, and within a matter of a week I was pleased to receive a reply indicating that consideration was being given. As Mr. Garneau said in his letter of September 28, 1955:
I am very pleased to state that the board has now come to the conclusion that, in accordance with the act, veterans of world war II who had actually left the shores of Canada before the 8th day of May 1945, and were on their way to an actual theatre of war, may be deemed to have been on service in a theatre of actual war outside the western hemisphere.
I have therefore advised the Vancouver district authority accordingly and I have no doubt that the case will now be dealt with solely on grounds of entitlement as otherwise provided for in the legislation.
The fact that it was dealt with on entitlement was, of course, an important factor and brought to my mind the thought that it is difficult to legislate for humanitarianism. I am sure the department will be pleased to know that the community of Langley in which this young man lived, as well as others who were interested in the case, including myself, are pleased with the work that was done and with the objective way in which this case was treated.

However, as in all departments, all cannot be said to be well so far as every phase is concerned. With respect to this department,
I view with some regret the loss of several trained appraisers we had in the New Westminster office of the Veterans' Land Act. I cannot help but think it is most difficult to replace some of these men from time to time.
I wonder whether they have been replaced, or whether it has been decided that we do not require replacements in the area.
I know there is a very heavy drain on trained personnel by private industry, which pays higher rates and also has other inducements such as the possibility of progression that is not experienced in governmental jobs, and which cannot be offered to civil servants from time to time. That applies particularly to the appraisers in this branch. Therefore I viewed with some concern the possibility that we might have lost some very competent men who were needed in the department.
The question of the plight of the wives of imperial war veterans whose husbands died before completing the 20-year period which would make them eligible for war veterans' allowances under the act was raised and has been raised for many years. In The Legionary magazine of April, 1956, I find on page 35 an article entitled, "A Happy Marriage". I am sure every hon. member here will be pleased to know that the marriage between the imperial veterans and the Canadian Legion has been consummated, for we feel satisfied that in unity lies strength. Possibly the strength of this new union will result in obtaining that which these widows have been trying to get for so many years. I well remember last year and previous occasions when they brought their brief before the committee and presented it in their capable way, and drew to our attention how necessary it was to try to do something for them. This article says in part:
We are, however, disappointed that the dominion government has not yet acted on the many representations requesting entitlement to the benefits of the War Veterans' Allowance Act for those widows of imperial and allied veterans whose service-husbands died before having established the 20-year qualifying residence period.
The article goes on:
We have evidence that the deceased commonwealth veterans for whose widows we now seek help, died in many cases only months and, in some cases, actually only weeks before having lived in Canada for the 20-year qualifying residence period.
Surely we should be in a position to give greater recognition to the few who are left, who have lived here for so many years. Surely we can prove that we in Canada are not as completely hard-hearted as this article would make us out to be. According to the best figures we can obtain there are
Supply-Veterans Affairs only a matter of some 500 to 750 who remain who might be eligible for an allowance. I am sure that many of them are in receipt of the old age pension at this time. Certainly it would not add too materially to the cost if we were to give these widows an allowance under the act as it might be revised. It is not a credit to our country to remain so unrealistic on this point and to be so dogmatic as to insist that because we have not given it up to this time we therefore should not give it in the future. I am satisfied, Mr. Chairman, that if a resolution were brought into this house by the government and a free vote were taken on the question, it would probably receive the greatest support of any piece of legislation that has come before the house to date.
From time to time in committee we have discussed the question and have heard from the ladies who brought the request to our attention. Their request has the support of other Legion groups. On no occasion was there any indication that any party or individual party member would be opposed to granting the assistance asked for by these ladies. It is my sincere hope that this "happy marriage," as it is referred to in this article, will mean this very thing; that it will present the matter in such a light to the government that it will no longer deny these widows that which I believe they have a right to expect.
It was not so very long ago-in fact on November 10,	1950-that the Canadian
Legion, dominion command, in presenting its brief to the Prime Minister made such a recommendation in these terms:
That widows of allied ex-service men be granted war veterans' allowance in cases where the husband died before completing 20 years' residence in Canada provided-(a) that the effective date of her eligibility be 20 years after the husband's arrival to take up permanent residence in Canada, (b) that the widow herself has completed 20 years' residence in Canada, and (c) that the husband and wife were both otherwise eligible.
The brief at that time pointed out that in many cases the husband may have lived in Canada for a lengthy period of time, paid Canadian taxes and seen his sons and daughters serve in the armed forces of this country. What the brief possibly did not point out was that although the husband may have predeceased the wife he did show good intentions in wanting to stay here, in which case, of course, he would continue to be a taxpayer. Because of the fact that many receive the old age pension today, because there are probably only between 500 and 750 who would be eligible, and because I am satisfied there would be no opposition in this house at least, to such a move if it were proposed by the govern-
5760	HOUSE OF
Supply-Veterans Affairs ment, I would sincerely urge the minister and the government to consider these factors and grant these people the assistance they have a right to expect.
There is one other matter with which I should like to deal. These matters appear to be minor, and if a committee on veterans' affairs had been set up we probably could have discussed them there more effectively. This is a matter, however, relating to the administration of the War Veterans' Allowance Act. While my time is somewhat limited and I do not wish to spend too much of it on this question, I did note that the minister in making his statement indicated that he had asked for a review of the administration and the application in respect to this assistance fund. He went on to say it would be applicable to those who cannot supplement their allowance through casual earnings.
I was pleased to hear him say that, because these are the people who are most in need of assistance. They have no means of obtaining casual earnings, and I was therefore particularly delighted to hear the minister make that statement. The fact is it has been suggested that probably the fund should be made available automatically to those people if the officials find they are incapable of obtaining casual earning.
Another problem which exists in my own province, because we have a health plan there, is the question of working out some plan with the government of British Columbia to make the terms of the hospital insurance act applicable to those who receive war veterans' allowance, on the same basis as if they were old age pensioners. At the present time the hospital insurance act does not give assistance to those who are in receipt of war veterans' allowance, and it therefore creates a hardship on those people when they go into our provincial hospitals. I am satisfied that if the minister or his officials were to see the department of health in my province in all likelihood they could arrive at some mutually satisfactory and amicable solution.
Another problem which has arisen and caused me some concern is the question of the comfort allowance. I have a case in mind in which a patient was in hospital on two separate occasions, the dates of which are important. The two occasions amounted to a full period of about seven weeks. The dates were from March 29 to April 16, and later from April 30 to May 29. As I understand it, under clause-12 treatment it is customary for a patient to be eligible for comfort allowance of $7 per month providing he is in hospital on or about the 27th of the month. He must be there, of course, to receive the cheque.


You will note that the first date was March 29, which was shortly after the 27th of the month. He left the hospital on April 16, before the end of the following month. This patient was not in hospital at a time which enabled him to appear on the list of those eligible for the comfort allowance cheque. On April 30, the date of his next entry into hospital, he was again not eligible because he came in too late; and while he was there on May 29 to be registered, he failed to collect because he was not there on the first of the month when the paymaster came around and he therefore received nothing. As I understand it, on an earlier occasion before the changes were made in the regulations the cheque would have been mailed out to him. Apparently that procedure is not being followed now and this patient was out of luck on both occasions because he happened to enter or depart from the hospital at an unfortuitous time.
The minister indicated, I believe, that the 1956 report is now being edited. There is one item in the report dated March 31, 1955, which interested me as it compared with the 1954 report. On page 11 of the 1955 report and on page 14 of the 1954 report are set out the number of veterans attending universities and vocational schools. We find that in 1954 there were 574 attending universities, which number had dropped to 377 in 1955. The 1956 report is not available as yet, but the indication is that the number attending universities is declining. The number attending vocational schools increased from 111 in 1954 to 346 in 1955. The over-all figures are 686 for 1954 and 713 for 1955.
There seems to be a definite trend toward the vocational schools, and I am wondering why the emphasis is that way, especially in view of the fact that we are so much in need of trained university graduates. Section 9 (1) (b) of the Veterans Rehabilitation Act states that a veteran must commence his course at university within one year and three months of his discharge.
The reason I raise this matter is that I have in mind the case of a young veteran who waited for a longer period before applying for assistance to go to university. Here again I must say that we have been told from time to time that we are in need of trained men, particularly those having vocational or university training. Such men are needed to aid us in our competition with communist countries. Yet this man has been refused the opportunity to attend university when he desires to do so, merely because application was not made within one year and three months after discharge.

I know this young man and I know he would be an asset to this country, even more so if he were fully trained rather than only partially trained as he is today. I would ask that the government review this section of the act. If it is felt that the act should not be changed, then I suggest that each case should be studied on its merits. With the initiative this young man has shown in past years, and with the ability I know he has, he could make a success of life. He simply wants to have that chance which is being denied him because the time limit has elapsed. I submit that these cases should be given special attention, and the act should provide for the consideration of each individual case.
I am satisfied that if that were done we would be in a position to continue to train many veterans in the future, and in so doing would soon be in a dominant position as far as education in this country is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to appear to be holding up my colleague's estimates, but in view of what he said in his excellent statement this afternoon and what other hon. members have said I think I should carry out an assignment which was given to me by a number of my fellow travellers last week on the very memorable trip we made to England. I should like to acknowledge, as I am sure the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich would if he were here, what was done for us.
I might note in passing that the hon. member is carrying out a mission of great importance and interest to veterans generally, near the city of Mons of armistice fame. In August, 1914 the British Lancers reached a point to the northeast of Mons and then began the retreat. On November 11, 1918 the third Canadian division surrounded Mons and the 116th Canadian battalion, commanded by Lt. Col. George Pearkes, V.C., reached exactly the same area as that which had been occupied by the Lancers. The regimental association of the 116th has since made a plaque which the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich is unveiling, with the co-operation of the Department of National Defence, on the 10th of this month. It will stand alongside a similar plaque of the 9th Lancers.
6, 1956	5761
Supply-Veterans Affairs
On the hon. member's behalf and on behalf of those whom the minister has mentioned I should like to express our appreciation to him and to his officials, both on this side and on the other side of the water. What was done was appreciated by the next of kin and all of us who had transportation arranged for us. There were other things done which were also greatly appreciated. Well before the time of departure officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs worked out detailed plans. An official accompanied the party over, and then on the other side arrangements were made which added greatly to the pleasure of everybody concerned.
I am sure the committee will be interested in knowing that those who were there as holders of the cross appreciated the fact that these arrangements had been made for the next of kin and relatives of those who had died. Everything was well arranged and the occasion was one of great importance and great significance. I should also say that the co-ordination between the Department of Veterans Affairs and the district administrator and his staff on the other side and the staff of the Department of National Defence on the other side was excellent. A bus was available at the hotel on every occasion, and either a representative of veterans affairs or a good staunch corporal of provost went through the hotel to make sure everyone got on the bus and got back safely on the return trip.
Last Sunday going down to Brookwood cemetery in the Bramshot area in the heavy rain such service was most noticeable and valuable. I should like to congratulate the minister and the department for the way their plans were carried out.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
